#6707. The Best Gifts Under $50 That Look Like a Splurge

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Because the perfect present doesn’t have to cost a fortune.

As I’ve been working through my holiday gifting list, I’ve come to realize it’s a little longer than anticipated—and the costs are already starting to add up. If you, too, have a long list of loved ones to shop for, stockings to fill, or simply want to keep your holiday spending in check, consider this your invitation to join me in seeking out budget-friendly presents that still feel thoughtful (and luxe).

I love nothing more than treating the people in my life to something I know they’ll treasure for years to come, but I’m not willing to sacrifice quality or thoughtfulness just to stick to a budget. Luckily, there’s no shortage of fabulous finds that look and feel far more expensive than their price tags suggest, from chunky mugs for sipping their favorite hot beverages and chic sweaters to bundle up in all season long to nourishing skin care that elevates their morning routines and clever tech gadgets that make everyday life a little easier.

Whether you’re shopping for a fashion or beauty lover, a devoted homebody, an avid entertainer, or someone who seems to have it all, you’ve come to the right place. Ahead, get a head start on crossing names off your list with thoughtful gifts that’ll make you their favorite gift-giver—all for under $50.

Elevate their everyday shower routine with a luxurious body wash that lathers beautifully and smells like an absolute dream.

You can’t go wrong with a little designer luxury, and this Chanel mascara is an ELLE editor favorite for its bold, volumizing effect.

Diptyque’s fragrances and candles always make for elegant gifts. This Fig Tree candle will fill their home with the captivating, woody aroma of fig trees, complemented by a hint of sweetness.

She’s bound to wear these dainty, everyday hoops on repeat, thanks to their versatile design and easy-to-use closures that mean no fussing with earring backs (or worrying about losing them).

A cozy sweater she can bundle up in all season long makes for a thoughtful gift, and this H&M find comes in the most gorgeous shade of burgundy.

How precious is this stoneware cocotte from Le Creuset? In the brand’s gorgeous Artichaut hue, it’s ideal for serving individual appetizers and baking side dishes or tasty desserts.

Elevate her space with a gleaming silver tray for displaying her favorite perfumes, jewelry, and other little treasures. For a personal touch, you can also have it engraved for an additional $17.

Whether she’s due for a new work bag or just needs a spacious handbag to carry her daily essentials, this refined H&M find looks far more expensive than its $40 price tag.

Give her jewelry collection a romantic addition with this statement chain necklace, complete with a hammered heart pendant that makes for a sweet declaration of your friendship.

Keep dry hands at bay with L’Occitane’s hand cream gift set, featuring five of the brand’s cult-favorite formulas. She can tuck one into each of her favorite handbags for extra nourishment whenever she needs it.

Fill her home with the intoxicating aroma of pumpkin and ginger courtesy of Apotheke’s reed diffuser, which doubles as a chic decorative accent.

Winter gloves are a must as temperatures plummet, and she’s sure to love this ultra-soft pair from Quince, crafted from Mongolian cashmere in the most charming Varsity Red color.

Whether she likes trying minis before committing to full-size products or is always on the go, treat her to this TSA-approved skin care set from Tower 28’s transformative SOS range. Inside, she’ll find a mini Hypochlorous Acid Spray, Barrier Repair Face Cream, and Gel Cleanser.

Help her drift off into a peaceful slumber with a luxurious weighted sleep mask designed to promote relaxation, so she can wake up feeling refreshed and ready to take on the day.

A limited-edition Gucci lipstick for exactly $50? Not only does it make for an unforgettable stocking stuffer, but I might just have to pick one up for myself, too.

Her post-shower routine is sure to feel more luxurious with Hommey’s ultra-absorbent hair wrap, which keeps wet hair neatly tucked away and prevents unwanted drips.

Treat her to a set of hydrating sheet masks she can reach for while lounging at home or prepping her skin before makeup application for a smoother, plumper-looking complexion.

Abbode has some of the sweetest embroidered gifts, including this tea towel adorned with a cheeky saying and cute martini motif.

Make her evening wind-down ritual a little cozier with this joyful set of four chunky mugs, giving her a lovely selection to choose from whenever she’s in the mood for a hot beverage.

Whether she layers the fragrances to create her own signature scent or wears each one on its own, Nicolaï Paris’s discovery set makes for a lavish gift that’ll have her thinking of you with every spritz.

#6705. Where to Stay in Jamaica for a Tropical Winter Sun Getaway

If you’re anything like me, entering the land of 4:50 p.m. sunsets means it’s time to a) cry a little and b) book a tropical vacation as soon as possible. In my experience, Jamaica has always been the perfect antidote to cold-weather blues; I’ve been nearly every winter for the past decade. This season, the island is still rebuilding after Hurricane Melissa made landfall last October, but its recovery—and tourism comeback—has been inspiring. Jamaica truly has it all, from iconic music and fashion to pristine beaches, lush rainforests, fresh (and absolutely delicious) food, and a long tradition of Hollywood and royal cachet.

As for where to stay? The boutique hotel scene is unmatched. While Jamaica does have its fair share of big-box, could-be-anywhere all-inclusives, the top hotels are the complete opposite and ooze charm.

Whether you want to drink rum punches on the cliffs of Negril, go hiking in the lush jungles of Port Antonio, or simply hang on the beach as the soft sounds of reggae drift through the air, these 12 options make it easy to experience the country’s vibrant creative culture for yourself. Just be prepared to get hooked, if you aren’t already.

Unless you live your life like a disgruntled White Lotus guest, it’s basically impossible to be in a bad mood at Rockhouse. Located on the western tip of Negril, the 40-room hotel—which celebrated its 50th anniversary in 2024—has all the ingredients for a good time. It’s built into Negril’s limestone cliffs, for starters, so the cliff jumping is next-level. The stone and thatched-roof villas are thoroughly charming; many of them have bright red ladders that allow you to climb directly down into the turquoise sea (which you should, especially first thing in the morning after a steaming mug of Blue Mountain coffee…heaven). The food is great, too, with fresh local dishes like callaloo omelets and moringa smoothies made with ingredients from the property’s on-site organic garden.

But really, you book this spot for the energy. Artists, designers, and other creatives frequent the property for its lively atmosphere and stylish crowd. I’ve personally stayed at Rockhouse twice myself—first with my mom and sister for a mother-daughter trip, and then with my two best friends for our 40th birthdays last year—and it was all smiles both times. My girlfriends and I still reminisce about our endless rum punches at the infinity pool bar, where the bartenders were so much fun, we momentarily forgot our bodies cannot handle mainlining cocktails like we once could. Luckily, that’s what hangover swims are for.

Amenities: three on-site restaurants, spa, infinity pool, weekly psilocybin sound bath experience, complimentary shuttles to Skylark Negril, daily morning yoga, candle-making workshops, and Rockhouse Foundation community tours

Bonus tip: The traditional bathing soak at the spa is heavenly: Tubs are filled with flower petals, herbs, botanicals, and your choice of aromatherapy oil.

Address: West End Road, Negril, Westmoreland

While the cliffs at Rockhouse are undoubtedly delightful, sometimes you just want to spend the day on the sand. And for that, Skylark—which opened as Rockhouse’s sister property in 2018—is the perfect choice. The 43-room boutique hotel holds a prime location right on Seven Mile Beach; not just a beach, but the beach in Negril. Skylark’s spot in the sand stands out for its yellow-and-white striped umbrellas and aqua loungers that match the sea.

Venture past the beach and you’ll notice the hotel’s mod, tropical design. While Rockhouse leans more rustic, Skylark is a bit of a throwback, with a very retro Miami Beach feel (think: black-and-white checkered floors and pops of pastel pink). And then there’s the Miss Lily’s of it all. Back in 2011, the team behind Rockhouse opened the Jamaican restaurant in Soho to bring the spirit of Rockhouse back home to New York, where it quickly acquired a cult following. So when Skylark announced it would open the first Miss Lily’s outpost in Jamaica itself, the superfans went wild—myself included. I’ve been twice now, and must say it feels extra special to enjoy their signature jerk chicken with a side of tropical breeze. Once the sun goes down, DJs take over with nightly sets of the country’s latest reggae and dancehall.

Amenities: rooftop spa, complimentary beach loungers, tents, and umbrellas, boutique and gift shop, beachside service from Miss Lily’s, daily shuttle to sister hotel Rockhouse

Bonus tip: Don’t miss the boutique’s Sweet Like JAM section, featuring high-end designers from across the African and Caribbean diaspora (like Diotima, Tribe Nine Studios, Theophilio, and Bianca Saunders), all curated by stylist and fashion editor Mecca James-Williams.

Address: Norman Manley Boulevard, Negril, Westmoreland

The secret’s certainly out about Geejam. This secluded hilltop hideaway is located in Port Antonio, a port town on Jamaica’s lush, lesser-visited northeastern coast. Built by two former music executives as a residential recording studio in 1998, the property eventually expanded into a boutique hotel in 2008 and has hosted everyone from Bad Bunny to Rihanna to Amy Winehouse (to Drake, Megan Thee Stallion, Harry Styles, Florence and the Machine, The Rolling Stones…the list goes on).

But despite its celeb appeal, Geejam somehow retains has the feel of an undiscovered gem. There are four wooden jungle cabins (named Ska, Rocksteady, Mento, and Drum & Bass, after Jamaica’s popular music genres), 12 guestrooms, a three-bedroom villa, and two premium villas with a dedicated staff. Many are built into the property’s six acres of rainforest so discreetly, you could miss them if you’re not looking. The main open-air bar and lounge, Bushbar, is just as low-profile: When my husband and I dropped in for a cocktail on a recent visit to “Portie,” (as the locals call it) we wondered if we were in the right place. A few guests were playing pool on the vintage billiard table, others were milling about the actual pool deck, and mellow reggae was playing softly in the background. Surely, we thought, a hotel this legendary would feel a bit more…scene-y? But of course, that understated vibe is precisely the point. It extends to the property’s new restaurant and bar, Bentley’s, which opened on their private, tucked-away beach in 2025 and serves a mix of Jamaican specialties and homemade pizza.

Amenities: recording studio, private beach with kayaking and paddleboarding, outdoor infinity pool, two main restaurants/bars, spa services, gym with private trainers available to book, pool table, treehouse DJ booth, various wedding and event spaces

Bonus tip: Portland is known for its waterfalls, rainforest hikes, river rafting, and iconic spring-fed Blue Lagoon—so tempting as it may be to hole up in your cabin, be sure to explore a little, too (the hotel’s custom excursions team can help with that). Don’t miss fresh lobster from Cynthia’s on Winnifred Beach; just call her a day ahead to place your order.

Address: 122 Skippers Boulevard, Port Antonio, Portland

Most people who visit Jamaica tend to stick to the main coastal towns of Negril, Montego Bay, Ocho Rios, and Port Antonio. But the country’s lush Blue Mountains—home to the legendary, eponymous coffee—are worth adding to your itinerary, too. And there is no better introduction to their misty magic than Strawberry Hill.

Set on a former coffee plantation just 10 miles above Kingston, the hilltop retreat is the go-to hotel in the Blue Mountains. A trip here begins with a steep, 45-minute drive up from the city (the hairpin turns and winding rainforest roads are part of the fun), but it really kicks off once you take in the sweeping panoramas from the top. The 26-acre property is centered around a sleek infinity pool that overlooks Kingston and the Caribbean Sea. The pool area feels especially glamorous at night, thanks to the city’s twinkling lights in the distance and the sound of clinking silverware from the on-site restaurant (get the rum cake for dessert). All 12 Georgian-style cottages and villas also have verandas that overlook the mountains and gardens. And for the birders among us, Strawberry Hill is home to 24 endemic species of our favorite friends, including the Doctor Bird, the country’s national bird.

But the biggest allure may just be the music history. Island Records founder Chris Blackwell purchased Strawberry Hill in 1974, and his influence is felt throughout the hotel, from the gold and platinum records on the walls to the vintage black-and-white photos of Bob Marley and other artists (Marley actually recovered at Strawberry Hill after he was shot in 1976, and his time there famously inspired him to write “Natural Mystic” later on). My husband and I loved sitting at the bar with a Blackwell Rum Punch, naturally, and chatting with the bartender about all the other musicians who’ve stayed there through the years: Peter Tosh, Yoko Ono, Mick Jagger, and many more.

Amenities: infinity pool, mountainside spa, yoga pavilion, on-site restaurant, landscaped gardens, bar with a fireplace and vintage piano, hiking trails

Bonus tip: Order a pot of Blue Mountain coffee to your room each morning, and enjoy it on your veranda while soaking in the strong morning sun. There’s something about drinking Blue Mountain coffee straight from the source that just hits different.

Address: New Castle Road, Irish Town, St. Andrew

For those immersed in the Jamaican hotel scene, GoldenEye needs no introduction. The legendary property on Jamaica’s north coast is filled with lore, starting with its origin as James Bond author Ian Fleming’s private retreat, which he built in 1946. Today, the property is owned by none other than Island Records founder Chris Blackwell, who bought it in 1976 and later made it part of his Island Outpost portfolio (along with Strawberry Hill and The Caves in Negril).

Glitzy history aside, it would be hard to have a bad time at GoldenEye. The property is practically set up to lower your cortisol, with 45 accommodations spread across 52 acres that include lush tropical gardens, quiet beaches, and its star attraction: a protected lagoon. Whether you opt for a lagoon cottage with a private dock, a beach villa right on the sand, or Fleming’s villa itself (a splurge, to be sure), there is truly no bad option here. Guests can even kayak across the lagoon to their spa appointments.

Amenities: swimmable lagoon, two freshwater swimming pools, saltwater splash pool, spa, boutique, private beaches, tennis court, pickleball court, kayaks, stand-up paddleboards, snorkeling equipment, Sunfish and Hobie Cat sailboats, two on-site restaurants, one on-site bar

Bonus tip: Be sure to spend time at Bizot Bar, GoldenEye’s casual beach restaurant named after the late counter-cultural journalist Jean-François Bizot (who was good friends with Blackwell). The breezy soundtrack comes courtesy of Radio Nova, a Paris-based radio station founded by Bizot that plays an eclectic mix of world music.

Address: Race Course, Oracabessa, St. Mary

Owned and operated by the Morrow family for nearly 70 years, Jamaica Inn is filled with family traditions, like a succession of pet black labradors all named Shadow (the first Shadow dates back to the 1970s). The beach bar, Teddy’s, is named after longtime bartender Teddy Tucker, who joined in 1958. Many of the staffers have worked there for more than 30 years, and notable guests include Marilyn Monroe, Katharine Hepburn, and Winston Churchill.

All history aside, the hotel is also just a beautiful spot that lends itself to a properly lazy time. Located in Ocho Rios, a resort town on Jamaica’s north coast, it’s spread along a private beach often considered to be one of the best in the Caribbean, with 700 feet of soft golden sand and pristine turquoise waters. On top of that, all 55 suites, cottages, and beachfront bungalows have direct views of those waters—and many have private plunge pools as well. They even have a no-screen rule, meaning there aren’t any TVs, radios, or clocks in the rooms to remind you of life outside your seaside bubble (whether or not you choose to surrender your phone to that rule is up to you). If you can manage to pry yourself away from the “beach-eat-repeat” lifestyle, Jamaica Inn has an array of activities to explore, from James Bond film showings on the sand to a tour of the hotel’s cannabis farm partner, Jacana, which includes a lesson on the history of Rasta culture.

Amenities: outdoor pool, spa, croquet lawn, garden tours, daily afternoon tea presentation, yoga pavilion, library, boutique, fitness center, complimentary daily activities, nightly live music

Bonus tip: Music lovers must take a field trip to nearby Nine Mile, the birthplace of Bob Marley.

DJ and music producer Diplo once told Vogue that his personal style is “kind of random; it does whatever.” But judging from his private (yet rentable) retreat, Pompey, his design style is far more considered. Set on 62 acres of private land in lush Port Antonio, the eight-suite property—which opened in 2024—is more like a Brutalist creative compound than a hotel, one where everything is intentionally set up to help you channel Jamaica’s artistic spirit. There’s a recording studio, naturally, complete with professional gear, and an impressive list of extras, from ping pong and chess to a wet bar with stocked snacks and an outdoor wooden deck overlooking the rainforest. There’s also an outdoor yoga pavilion, an equestrian center, and a two-floor gym with wellness facilities including hydrotherapy, infrared sauna, and skincare treatments with products from the legendary Dr. Barbara Sturm. All stays come fully staffed with daily housekeeping and a full-time chef, who, instead of supplying menus, cooks based on the vibe of the day.

Designed by Brooklyn studio Freecell Architecture and architect Gia Wolff, the concrete retreat is meant to both blend into nature and look striking against it. Centered around a saltwater infinity pool, the property stretches out into a regenerative farm and orchard with all sorts of walking paths, ATV trails, and direct access to Port Antonio’s beautiful San San Beach. Even if you’re not blessed with a productive burst of creativity while you’re there, you’ll likely still leave feeling relaxed and at peace—a win, either way.

Amenities: recording studio, on-property helicopter access, saltwater infinity pool, yoga pavilion, gym, equestrian center, ATV access, E-bikes, walking paths, regenerative farm and orchard, concierge-led programming

Bonus tip: To book, email Pompey’s concierge directly through their website. Rooming configurations are quite flexible, so tell them exactly what you’re looking for and they will set you up accordingly—they can even arrange additional accommodations five minutes away for larger groups.

Address: Fairy Hill, Port Antonio, Portland

Mention Treasure Beach to anyone familiar with Jamaica, and they will likely think of Jakes. Since its opening in 1993, the 60-room boutique hotel has become something of a treasure in Treasure Beach—pun very much intended—and it’s not hard to see why. Founded by Jamaica-born artist and designer Sally Henzell, Jakes reflects her creative sensibility everywhere you look. The bungalows, cottages, villages and rooms are painted in a rainbow of colors, and they’re all decorated with local art. Like most of Jamaica’s south coast, Jakes was hit hard by Hurricane Melissa last year, but fortunately, it began welcoming guests again that December and fully reopened in March with reimagined oceanfront bungalows. Its whimsical design is still a big part of the appeal.

The other main appeal? Treasure Beach itself. Unlike some of Jamaica’s more tourism-oriented hubs like Montego Bay and Ocho Rios, Treasure Beach is quite low-key. There are a few guesthouses and restaurants, but mostly it’s just rocky coastline, houses that dot the fields, and splashes of magenta bougainvillea. No all-inclusives, no cruise ships. For book lovers, the property hosts the Calabash International Literary Festival every other May. It’s drawn a glittery crowd over the years, from authors (Zadie Smith, Marlon James, and Padma Lakshmi, to name a few) to guests including Angelina Jolie.

Amenities: private beach and dock, freshwater pool, three restaurants, ocean-facing spa, seaside yoga deck with daily sessions, gift shop, monthly full moon dinners, on-site art classes

Bonus tip: Take the complimentary boat trip to Floyd’s Pelican Bar, Treasure Beach’s iconic thatched-roof bar that sits on stilts in the middle of the sea. It was fully destroyed by Hurricane Melissa, but has since reopened.

Address: Calabash Bay, Treasure Beach, Saint Elizabeth

While Montego Bay has its fair share of standard all-inclusives, Round Hill is anything but. Set on 110 lush acres of former pineapple groves, the storied boutique has been the go-to spot for an elegant stay in the area since it opened in 1953. John F. Kennedy and Jackie Kennedy honeymooned there, and Meghan Markle and Prince Harry have visited, too. But no guest is more associated with the property than Ralph Lauren. He visited for the first time at Christmas in 1978 and loved it so much, he proceeded to buy two cottages there: High Rock in 1982, and White Orchid in 1996. In the early 2000s, Lauren even redesigned all 36 rooms in the main hotel (known as the Pineapple House), as well as the cocktail lounge, which is considered to be the original Polo Bar. His touch is evident in the country club style that runs throughout: white stone floors, four-poster mahogany bamboo beds, and the green-and-white striped awnings.

Aside from those 36 Pineapple House rooms Lauren designed, there are also 27 individually-owned villas, ranging from two to six bedrooms. Travelers also book Round Hill for its impeccable landscaping and fresh feel. It’s an extremely well-manicured resort, after all—one where lush gardens seem to stretch on for miles and open skies are never hard to find. Add an array of activities to the mix—including tennis, pickleball, and river rafting—plus island fare from the property’s 11 dining options, and you’ve got everything you need for an idyllic tropical stay.

Amenities: spa, fitness center and fitness classes, outdoor infinity pool, walking trail, water sports facility, house reef, boutique, chef’s garden, events pavilion, daily complimentary afternoon tea, nightly entertainment

Bonus tip: During the festive season, Round Hill hosts daily cocktail classes at 3 p.m., where you can learn about the history of Jamaican rum and Blue Mountain coffee—and make your own cocktails, of course.

Address: John Pringle Drive, Montego Bay, Hanover

Set on 400 acres along two miles of Montego Bay coastline, Half Moon has been a resort mainstay on Jamaica’s north shore since it opened in 1954. It’s known for its whitewashed cottages, wide verandas, and unmistakably grand feel. JFK stayed there (the man clearly loved Jamaica!), as did many members of the British royal family, including Queen Elizabeth II, then-Prince Charles, and Prince Harry. Sadly, because Half Moon is quite open to the elements, it was hit especially hard by Hurricane Melissa last year, which caused extensive damage to the property and personally affected more than 850 of its team members. Some villas reopened in April after a major restoration effort, but the historic resort just announced that most of the remaining property will reopen by Thanksgiving, followed by the final batch of cottages by the festive season. That includes a mix of rebuilds, redesigns, and new additions like Garlandstone Gallery, which will sell local art.

Half Moon is particularly strong in the tropical activity department: golf, tennis, pickleball, water sports, locally inspired spa treatments, and excursions that go deeper into Jamaican culture are all available. I especially loved the farm-to-table vegan dining experience at Stush in the Bush, an organic farm and restaurant in the lush fields of St. Ann. Think crispy plantain chips, wood-fired pizza, and skillet cornbread, all served with herbs from the garden and their own line of gourmet sauces and spreads.

Amenities: private beach, infinity pool, swimming coves and lagoon, spa, golf course, equestrian center, tennis and pickleball courts, water sports, sailing and diving classes, sea turtle releases, on-site garden, fitness studio, 10 bars and restaurants, children’s village

Bonus tip: The hotel’s collection of paintings from Montego Bay artist Michael Lester is now available for purchase. Lester, who died in 1972, is known for his expressionist paintings of Montego Bay and Jamaican life.

Address: Rose Hall, Montego Bay, St. James

Plus, the cabin itself is incredibly peaceful. With a lush garden filled with birds, plants scattered throughout the home, and exposed cedar beams in most rooms, it feels like a true city oasis. Perhaps best of all? The cabin is located directly under a mango tree, so you get a real taste of island living. (The owner, Terryon, may even greet you with a fresh mango smoothie.)

Amenities: Outdoor shower, HDTV, AC, backyard, outdoor dining furniture, hammock, free parking

If you’re looking for the perfect spot for a tropical group getaway, say for a birthday or a bachelorette, look no further than this massive Airbnb in Negril. Set beneath a grove of palm trees just steps from the famed Seven Mile Beach, it sleeps up to ten people and comes fully staffed with a private chef, butler, and housekeeper. There’s a gorgeous pool with loungers, and a large outdoor dining table perfect for long group dinners.

All five bedrooms come equipped with a four-poster king bed, private bathroom, private terrace, and ocean views—here, there is no surrendering to the “bad room” just to make someone else happy. There are also multiple hangout rooms for lounging, all with an airy, white-on-wood tropical design and colorful artwork on the walls. Reviewers are especially into the butler service, with one saying her butler would just “appear at the beach” with a carafe of hot coffee anytime hers was running low (Jamaican hospitality at its finest). And to really take any possible friction out of your group stay, you can even arrange for the kitchen to come pre-stocked at an additional cost.

Amenities: Chef and cleaning available during stay, pool, AC, washer, TV, bar, outdoor furniture, beachfront access, kayak, free parking

#6703. Joseph Zada of The Hunger Games Is Still Getting Used to Being a Movie Star

Joseph Zada is doing “very, very, very good,” he tells me, with a heavy emphasis on the third very and an audible exclamation mark. And why shouldn’t he be?

His much-anticipated film, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, finally comes out this week. Zada and I spoke the morning of his New York City premiere, while he was being shuttled from one press obligation to the next, already go-go-go before actually hitting the red carpet Monday night in custom Louis Vuitton, punctuated with a pair of gold-toed cowboy boots from Pharrell’s first collection for the brand.

In the film, Zada plays a young Haymitch Abernathy, who we follow through his own Hunger Games, some twenty-five years ahead of the events of the original trilogy. When asked about the movie, the 21-year-old Australian demonstrates palpable care and excitement, even a bit of sadness that it’s over. “I just think that it was the most I’ve had to prepare and the most support that I’ve had and the most that I’ve ever stepped into a character’s shoes,” Zada says. “And it was just such a joy to act in this and to feel what it was like to really be this character.”

Since being cast, he’s barely had a second to stop and reflect on joining one of the biggest franchises in the world—and this comes right on the heels of East of Eden, too, in which Zada played another haunted young man. He laughs when I note the comparison: “I guess I just pride myself on my ability to show my vulnerability.”

Below, read our full conversation with the emerging star as he reflects on his Hunger Games journey, talks red carpet style, and shares his thoughts on Robert Pattinson playing James Bond.

Joseph Zada: Yeah, I wonder if I’ll be nervous.

Maybe towards the start. It doesn’t get old… but it gets familiar.

Well, I did SiriusXM this morning, and then, I mean, it’s basically just been like, "Hey, do press all day and then go to your premiere." So there’s not much time for a ritual, so I guess I go a little bit nonverbal and half-dissociate.

No, it’s so much fun. I have a lot of fun at these premieres. It’s always like a crazy, crazy crowd. The way they’ve set it up has just been otherworldly, and I’m not sure if I’ll ever have it again, but I distinctly remember each stop and the feelings that I’ve had thus far, and it doesn’t get old. It’s always crazy to see this many fans and the passion they have for this project. I mean, it’s not every day that you get to step into something with a built-in fan base where people are already coming out and supporting it before they’ve even seen it. So it’s a really special experience, and I don’t know when I’m going to be able to get that again.

Where did I have the most fun? I had a lot of fun in London because my little sister was there, my little sister and my brother’s girlfriend, so I got to hang out with them and I haven’t seen them in a while. And Mexico. Mexico was the craziest event that we’ve had. There were literally thousands, several thousands of people there. The reception was incredible.

Am I allowed to drop this? Oh, yes, that is what this [interview] is for. I’m wearing a Louis Vuitton suit—custom, custom—that Jason [Bolden] and I have worked together on, and I’m a big fan of the boots. The boots are pretty dope.

I feel a lot more comfortable in these clothes nowadays, and it’s actually become a lot more enjoyable to put them on. And it feels like more of an armor and less of a scary thing, and it feels like I build a lot of confidence being able to do this.

My red carpet style, I think... I don’t know. Just whatever Jason puts me in for the night.

Yeah, I think just doing it so often and finding different looks and just being able to wear all the different brands and find what I’m comfortable in.

I pride myself on my ability to have vulnerability. I think as a young man, that’s what I find interesting in these performances of these young men coming of age, and I think that was really what I was just looking for in my early career. I modeled my career on people like Timothée Chalamet and Lucas Hedges, and I love the way that they kept their heart on their sleeve and how they feel like an open nerve. I love being able to portray that in my performances.

I just think that it was the most I’ve had to prepare and the most support that I’ve had and the most that I’ve ever stepped into a character’s shoes and really, really felt like I was there every single day and just had the most incredible support in terms of my cast mates and my directors and my producers. And it was just such a joy to act in this and to feel what it was like to really be this character.

I guess everything just kind of changed just like that. Everything just changed in one quick second, and it feels like... I guess I haven’t really thought about what it was like before. I’ve just kind of been trying to ride the wave. I’m sure being able to go back home for Christmas, I’ll have some time to reflect, but right now it’s just—what’s the day ahead of me? And just making sure I’m ready for all of that.

I’m just excited to be at home every single day and watch movies with my mom and my siblings and see all my friends. That’s what I’m really excited for. I’m just excited to also just turn off my phone for a little bit, maybe go on a little road trip down to South Australia and get a little beach house and not bring my phone and have six days where I’m just off the grid.

That’s a great question. I’ve got Apocalypse Now on 4K Ultra HD on my projector that I bought at home, and I cannot wait. I feel like people ask me what was the best part of my year, and I just start naming all the movies that I’ve watched. And genuinely the happiest that I ever am is when I’m watching a film, which is kind of sad but also kind of cool.

I think... I don’t know. I loved Wild Horse Nine. That’s a favorite I’ve watched in cinemas. I loved Primetime too, because I love Rob Pattinson. I love Skyler Gisondo.

I did just see the Bond casting news! I am chuffed. That is so exciting. That is beyond exciting. He is just the most phenomenal actor, and he really just makes the most interesting choices. And I think him in that role, the stoicism that he’ll bring along with those really interesting choices, it’s going to make that character so interesting. He’s a really special actor. It feels like every young male actor that I speak to feels like that is a person to look to right now and a person’s career to emulate in terms of the risks and the commitment to his craft and all these roles that he’s churning out.

I don’t know. It’s so ridiculously helpful to have a book with you because it’s just so much information, and I love preparing for roles and having a book because it’s just an internal monologue, which is what you should be doing for every character. You read a scene, and you should be writing what is going through your character’s head. And when you have a book, it’s all done for you, or at least you have a good foundation.

I hope I get to do as many book adaptations as possible, but I think what I’m really looking for is just a great director and a great script. I’m not sure what’s [next]. I’ve got a fresh slate right now, but there’s a couple of things floating around.

#6702. 5 Restaurant Chains With Troubling Food Safety Records

Let's just say the health department had a few notes.

Not every day can be a home-cooked meal kind of day. Sometimes, going out really pays off. It saves you time in the kitchen, cuts down on effort, and most importantly, lets you relax while someone else does the heavy lifting. Many families turn to fast food when they want an easy, quick meal or when time is of the essence. But where you go can really make a difference.

Admittedly, fast food chains don’t always have the best reputation, especially when it comes to health concerns. But beyond the macros, another factor to consider is cleanliness.

Cleaning protocols differ from chain to chain—and even from location to location. You may have seen headlines concerning less-than-stellar hygiene reports stemming from certain fast food locations over the years. Kitchen cleanliness is paramount to food safety (just look at this year’s Cyclospora outbreak), and some chains have faced more than their share of troubling headlines. Here are five fast food chains with a disappointing history of food safety issues.

I hate to break it to burrito-with-extra-guac fans, but Chipotle has a history of high-profile food safety issues. The company paid $25 million to resolve criminal charges related to a series of foodborne illness outbreaks between 2015 and 2018. According to the documents, Chipotle was charged with "adulterating food in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act," resulting in the largest criminal fine ever imposed in a food safety case at the time.

Records cited at least five foodborne illness outbreaks across several states, including incidents involving norovirus, that sickened more than 1,100 people. These outbreaks "primarily stemmed from store-level employees' failure to follow company food safety protocols." Personally, I'd rather have a side of hot sauce than a side of stomach flu.

In February 2025, a Massachusetts store was cited for nine core health code violations—including insufficiently cleaned ice machines, improperly stored produce, and missing thermometers in a walk-in cooler—along with one priority foundation violation. Such issues can raise concerns about food safety and sanitation.

In 2022, a health inspector described another location in the state as "very unclean." A year before that, workers at a Springfield, Missouri, location staged a walkout over poor working conditions. A subsequent health inspection found that "the floors in the food preparation area (especially under equipment and near drains), walk-in refrigerator and freezer, and dry storage areas were not clean," leading to a follow-up inspection. (Don't even get us started on some of the issues found overseas!)

Sorry, chalupa lovers. Taco Bell has also faced its share of food safety concerns over the years. Reports include an E. coli outbreak along the East Coast in 2006 resulting in 71 illnesses (53 of whom were hospitalized), two Salmonella outbreaks in 2010 affecting at least 155 people across 21 states, and a hepatitis A outbreak in 2000 that sickened 23 people and hospitalized 15.

More recently, a customer’s viral video appeared to show a Taco Bell kitchen strewn with food, garbage, and old boxes near food prep areas. Some commenters suggested that it was filmed during rush hour while the restaurant was understaffed and that employees were too busy to clean. Still, it's not a great look for in-store hygiene.

Big Mac lovers, look away. The Golden Arches have faced numerous lawsuits over food safety issues over the years, including a class action suit (plus several personal injury suits) filed in 2024 following a multistate E. coli outbreak linked to Quarter Pounders. The outbreak ultimately sickened 104 people and killed one, with investigators identifying slivered onions as the likely source of contamination.

The Boston City Department of Inspectional Services found nearly 125 violations at seven different McDonald's locations between 2018 and 2019—everything from mismanaged storage to mold, rat droppings, and even live cockroaches. Complaints and lawsuits have also alleged undercooked meat and foodborne illnesses caused by cross-contamination.

Wendy's locations have racked up numerous health code violations, too (one Las Vegas restaurant in particular drew 27 demerits in a 2019 inspection for dirty soda nozzles, food left on the floor, raw food cross-contamination, and more). A 2023 "Dirty Dining" segment called out a Fort Lauderdale, Florida, location with an inspection that found insects all over the restaurant.

Perhaps most concerningly, a Michigan family filed a lawsuit in 2024 alleging their daughter developed hemolytic uremic syndrome following an E. coli infection they attributed to food from Wendy's. According to the lawsuit, the illness caused permanent brain damage, kidney failure, a seizure disorder, and other lasting health problems. Inspectors had found the location in violation of 17 different health and food codes just days before the family's visit, including moldy food, spoiled produce, dirty surfaces, and water leaks.

Even with these histories of violations, not every location should make you rethink your dining options—many restaurants are up to code and clean. While all this information is enough to convince me to stick to home-cooked meals for the rest of my life, I suggest checking your local restaurant's latest health inspection report before deciding whether or not to visit your chain of choice.

#6700. Vogue’s 16 Best Hotels in the Alps, From Chic Chalets to Design-Forward Boutique Stays

The Alps have a particular hold on the imagination. There are the snow-dusted peaks, naturally, and the villages tucked into their folds, with timber chalets, candlelit restaurants, and views that could make even the most committed city dweller reconsider their priorities. But the pleasures of an Alpine escape extend well beyond a day on the slopes and unlimited raclette.

Across France and Switzerland, the region’s hotels run the gamut from storied grand dames and old-world mountain inns to contemporary retreats where thoughtful architecture and considered design take center stage. Some trade in old-school glamour, others in rustic charm or a welcome degree of seclusion, but the best are worth giving up a powder morning for and staying in. Whether you’re here for serious skiing, fireside dinners, or simply the pleasure of waking up to a panorama of peaks, these are the Alpine hotels in France and Switzerland worth planning a trip around this winter.

Les Fermes de Marie, a hamlet above Megève, was put together in 1989 by Jean-Louis and Jocelyne Sibuet from Savoyard farm buildings dismantled elsewhere and carted here, stone by stone. The result is a welcome abundance of old timber, antiques, wool, plaid, and animal skins, with fires burning in the appropriate places. (The Sibuets also run La Bastide de Marie in the Luberon and Villa Marie in Saint-Tropez, but this is their grande dame; no small thing from a family this good at hospitality, especially where children are concerned.) Here, they are dispatched to Le Hameau des Enfants, a free club with its own children’s concierge, where 5-to-10-year-olds are kept busy with cooking and ski lessons.

Breakfast, served in the heart of the hotel, in the main restaurant with an enormous fireplace, is not to be slept through (on the menu: homemade jams, Alpine cheeses, farm butter, and exceptional bread). From 2 to 6 p.m. the lounges and library put out homemade Savoie cakes, whipped-cream waffles and the house hot chocolate, after which the bar moves on to wine with slates of local cheese and charcuterie. By evening the main dining room settles into traditional Savoyard cooking by the fire, including a house pâté that has earned its permanent place on the menu. Downstairs, the hotel’s stube is given over entirely to cheese—fondue included—though for dinner in town, the family also owns Le Vieux Megève, a Savoyard institution in the village with as many locals at its tables as guests. The spa’s outdoor hot tubs are best used in falling snow, when the hamlet looks sealed inside a snow globe, and the terraces come heaped with sheepskins and blankets for an evening apéritif under the heat lamps.

Amenities: Spa, restaurants, pool, kids’ club, shuttle, on-site ski rental

Editor’s tip: Stop by L’Épicerie de Megève, the Sibuets’ grocery in the village. The breakfast jams are on the shelves, as is honey from the hotel’s own hives and wine from the family’s Luberon estate, all of which makes for a perfect souvenir.

Address: 163 Chemin des épis, 74120 Megève

The Saint-Georges is the latest addition to Megève’s hospitality scene. Located right in the center of Megève, a few steps from the pedestrian rue Charles Feige and a short walk from the lifts, the old building has been reimagined by the English designer Luke Edward Hall as a kind of Alpine fairy tale, complete with all the decorative flourishes that the genre demands.

Savoyard folklore provided the starting point, but the 29 rooms take the idea in a cheerfully eccentric direction: Pierre Frey fabrics, painted and patterned headboards, boldly colored bathrooms, floral tiles, deep carpets, and hand-painted murals jostle against carved wood and antiques. On weekend evenings, there’s live piano beside the fire in the bar, lending the place the air of an old mountain inn in which one might reasonably expect a wolf, a princess, or at least a particularly off-kilter uncle to appear before dinner. Le Trappeur, the hotel’s bistro, serves classic French cooking with a few Savoyard dishes, while the spa takes a more elemental approach, built around hot and cold contrast therapy. Families are well catered to, with dedicated rooms and activities for children who may find themselves rather more at home here than in the usual hushed Alpine palace.

Amenities: Spa, restaurant, bar, kids’ club

Address: 159, Rue Monseigneur Conseil, 74120 Megève

Le Coucou occupies a large wooden chalet on Méribel’s Belvédère, beside the Rond-Point des Pistes, arranged so that the windows look out over the slopes and a blue run begins just beyond the ski room. It is ski-in, ski-out in the fullest sense: Staff are on hand to unbuckle your boots, lest the final indignity of the day prove too much.

On arrival, one encounters a domed ceiling painted by Matthieu Cossé with owls perched among trees against blue mountain peaks, which establishes the level of seriousness with which the decor is to be taken. Pierre Yovanovitch designed more than 130 pieces of furniture and lighting for the 55 rooms and public spaces—including teddy-shaped armchairs—and set them among terracotta walls, sheepskin, and upwards of 160 artworks, Calder and Chillida included. The bar, done up in yellow, blue, and cream, looks directly onto the pistes through floor-to-ceiling windows. There are indoor and outdoor pools, a Tata Harper spa, and two children’s clubs, should the adults require a little peace. For dinner, Biancaneve serves Italian food; Le Fumoir seats sixteen around a fireplace for fondue; their flagship restaurant Beefbar extends onto a terrace. The whole enterprise is unapologetically theatrical; and though one might reasonably ask how much theater a ski holiday requires, the answer, apparently, is quite a lot.

Amenities: Spa, restaurants, bar, pools, kids’ clubs, ski-in, ski-out, on-site ski rental

Address: 464 Route du Belvédère 73550 Les Allues Méribel

Courchevel has never been short of hotels willing to make a spectacle of luxury. Saint Roch, opening in December on the Bellecôte piste, is Maisons Pariente’s case for the opposite approach, one the family already made persuasively in Paris with Le Grand Mazarin and Méribel’s Le Coucou. Architects Virginie Friedmann and Delphine Versace have recast a longstanding hotel as something closer to a well-traveled aesthete’s chalet, its 37 rooms dressed in dark wood, mohair velvet, agate and onyx by way of Russian dachas and Persian interiors. Pierre Mesguich’s mosaic frescoes and Atelier Toporkoff’s stained glass do more for the place than any amount of gilt would. The living room alone, with its deep sofas and fireplace, makes a decent case for skipping the afternoon session.

Come evening, visit Prunier, the Parisian caviar house’s first alpine restaurant. To unwind further, head downstairs, where you’ll find a ceramic-tiled pool and Tata Harper treatments that take their cue from Ottoman hammams.

Amenities: Spa, pool, ski shop, ski-in, ski-out, on-site ski rental

Address: Piste de Bellecote, 73120 Courchevel 1850

Opening in December from Chapitre Six, the group behind Megève’s Saint-Georges, Bourbon Hotel seems to have concluded that the last thing the resort needs is another chalet. Instead, it takes its cues from a London members’ club, with dark woods, deep velvets, and low lighting. It sits in Courchevel’s Golden Triangle, with direct ski-in, ski-out access to Les Trois Vallées, which is useful, though the more interesting offerings involve what happens after a day on the slopes.

Simonetta, the hotel’s Italian restaurant, will be led by Simone Zanoni, whose Paris credentials include Le George at the George V; this will be his first restaurant in the mountains. The bar pairs cocktails with vinyl sessions, a combination that suggests the après-ski hours here are to be taken at least as seriously as the skiing itself. Below ground, a spa built around contrast therapy offers the usual opportunity to repair the damage before heading out to do it all again. There are 28 rooms and three suites, and pets are permitted on request. Whether Bourbon can make the London-club formula work at altitude remains to be seen, but it is at least a departure from the expected wood-and-antler routine.

Amenities: Spa, restaurant, bar, ski-in, ski-out

Address: 286 Rue Park City, 73120 Courchevel

Les Airelles occupies the Place de Neige, where the village meets the mountain, with direct access to the pistes and the Solaise and Olympique gondolas, as well as a large sun terrace for watching skiers descend. Its 41 rooms, suites, and penthouses have been conceived in the spirit of a medieval Alpine residence, furnished with antiques and artworks drawn from a collection of more than 4,000 pieces. Each has a balcony or terrace, and the penthouses come with their own butler. The Bernard Orcel ski room takes care of the business of getting dressed for the mountain, and, on one’s return, offers hot drinks and crêpes. Dinner can be had at Matsuhisa or Palladio, followed by a stint in the Guerlain spa—the largest in Val d’Isère–or the private cinema.

Children have a grotto-like pool of their own, while dogs receive monogrammed mats, personalized collars, and a dedicated walker to take them out while their owners ski. There is something delightfully over-the-top about a hotel that provides more elaborate arrangements for a dog’s afternoon than most people make for their own, but Les Airelles has never been especially interested in the modest pleasures of Alpine life. Its particular talent is to turn every practical inconvenience into an occasion for service, and every stay into a small performance of aristocratic excess.

Amenities: Spa, restaurants, pools, cinema, ski-in, ski-out, on-site ski rental

Address: 145 Rue de la Poste, 73150 Val d'Isère

The skiing is serious in Verbier, but so is the après. Experimental, the Paris group that built its reputation on cocktail bars, chose its first Alpine hotel accordingly, opening a chalet a short walk from the lifts and directly above Farm Club; otherwise known as the nightclub that has kept the village awake since 1971.

For those who have come to ski, the village shop Les Ruinettes delivers rentals to heated lockers downstairs, and a shuttle takes guests to the lifts. The 39 rooms, designed by Fabrizio Casiraghi, favor warm wood, deep colors, and clean lines over the typical heavy chalet style. This ethos extends to the food: Saint Bernard, the restaurant beside reception, gives Alpine classics a lighter touch. Upstairs, the Experimental Cocktail Club draws a mixture of hotel guests and outsiders, while the outdoor hot tub at the Biologique Recherche spa looks directly into the bar, allowing one to order a cocktail through the window without ever getting out of the tub. Starting this November, the bar is introducing a vinyl listening room built around Klipsch speakers, where record selectors stand in for the usual resort DJ.

Amenities: Spa, restaurant, bars, nightclub, hot tub, ski lockers, shuttle

Editor’s tip: On certain weeknights, guests can bring their own records to play in the new listening bar.

Address: Route de Verbier Station 55, 1936 Verbier

Welsh brothers Grant and Craig Maunder, who have been part of Adelboden since Grant first came here in the late seventies, own two hotels in the village; the Brecon, named for the Brecon Beacons, is the smaller, quieter one, housed in a timber building dating to 1914 at the more peaceful end of town. Its interiors look to the ’50s and ’60s, with leather, wool, stone, and crazy-paved Welsh slate underfoot. (Continuing the nod to the owners’ home, you’ll also find Welsh wool blankets lie folded on the beds.)

Each of the 18 rooms and four lofts are television-free; a decision that might once have seemed a little severe but becomes easier to defend when you realize the Adelboden massif occupying the entire window offers a much better thing to stare at. Grant’s wife, the American ceramicist Andrea Anderson, has thrown more than 950 pieces of pottery by hand for the hotel, a level of commitment to the breakfast table that seems almost unreasonable until one sees the results. The Brecon is adults-only and all-inclusive, organized around an open kitchen, with a sauna facing the mountains. While it’s not ski-in, ski-out, a free shuttle runs to the lifts, and a heated Art Deco pool awaits on your return.

Amenities: Restaurant, sauna, pool, shuttle

Editor’s tip: As an all-inclusive adults-only property, food, drinks, and spa access are included in the room rate.

At Kleine Scheidegg, beneath the Eiger, the Mönch, and the Jungfrau, the day ends when the last train leaves. The pass is accessible only by the Wengernalp railway, and once the final service has departed, the guests of the Bellevue des Alpes have the mountain largely to themselves.

The inn has stood here for generations: Christian Seiler bought it in 1840, and his descendants, the von Almens, still run it, with Andreas von Almen and his wife Silvia (a flutist), representing the fifth generation. The hotel was last extended in 1948, and little in the public rooms seems to have felt an urgent need for improvement since then. There is the grand piano, the old furnishings, and a bar dating to 1929, its swing door hung with photographs of the climbers and guides who used the hotel as a base camp for attempts on the Eiger’s north face. Guests would watch their progress through telescopes on the terrace, a rather more compelling form of entertainment than anything likely to appear on a hotel television. Clint Eastwood filmed The Eiger Sanction here in 1974, though the mountain itself has never needed Hollywood to establish its credentials. Skiing begins at the front door, and the setting is so imposing that the usual question of what else the hotel offers seems faintly beside the point.

Amenities: Restaurant, bar, terrace, ski-in, ski-out

Klosters acquired its Hollywood connections after the war, when American soldiers interned in Switzerland returned with their families and friends, and the film business followed. Greta Garbo, Gene Kelly, and Rex Harrison all appear in the guest book at the Chesa Grischuna, which earned the nickname “Hollywood on the Rocks”. The Guler family opened the hotel in 1938, and since 2022 it has been run by Zurich entrepreneurs Astrid von Stockar and Clemens Gregor. The entire building is a protected landmark, listed on Switzerland’s national register of historic places.

The thirteen rooms are furnished with antiques and local woodwork, and the old piano bar, whose walls are painted with winter scenes, is now a pasta bar—the natural gathering place after a day on the slopes. But the hotel’s best surprise lies below: a two-lane bowling alley painted by Alois Carigiet, the Swiss illustrator best known for A Bell for Ursli. Raclette is served in the adjoining tavern, which seems an entirely sensible way to recover from an evening of competitive bowling. One can understand why the Hollywood contingent came back: The Chesa Grischuna offers the sort of atmosphere that no amount of set dressing can quite manufacture, and has managed to preserve it without turning its history into a theme park.

Amenities: Restaurants, bar, bowling alley

Address: Bahnhofstrasse 12, 7250 Klosters-Serneus

Sils Maria has attracted writers and painters for well over a century. (Nietzsche among them: His summer house stands directly across the road from Chesa Marchetta.) The village lies between the lakes of Sils and Silvaplana, just fifteen minutes from St. Moritz, though it belongs to a rather different tradition of Engadin life—one more interested in contemplation than conspicuous consumption.

Chesa Marchetta occupies four connected farmhouse buildings dating to the sixteenth century. Artfarm, the hospitality company founded by Swiss gallerists Iwan and Manuela Wirth, whose other projects include Scotland’s Fife Arms, spent four years restoring the property before reopening it in January. The architect Luis Laplace retained the original sgraffito—the intricate scratched-plaster decoration that distinguishes the old houses of the valley—and furnished the thirteen rooms with traditional Engadin furniture, antiques, and work by local artists and artisans. Art, in other words, is not an accessory here so much as part of the building’s grammar.

Upstairs, the library and bar form the social heart of the house, a richly layered room where books, beautiful works of art and carefully chosen furnishings make for an atmosphere closer to a collector’s private residence than a conventional hotel lounge. It is the sort of place that invites you to linger over a drink, surrounded by objects with their own stories, without ever feeling overly designed. Downstairs, the restaurant draws on seasonal recipes, an Italian-Swiss mixture that makes good sense in a valley whose geography has never entirely respected national borders. Lake Sils is a fifteen-minute walk away, while Corvatsch is the nearest skiing.

Address: Via da Marias 88, 7514 Sils im Engadin/Segl

There are luxury hotels, and then there are institutions whose very existence has helped define luxury. Badrutt’s Palace, which opened in 1896, belongs rather emphatically to the latter category, having spent more than a century establishing the terms of alpine grandeur. Its unmistakable tower rises above the center of St. Moritz, overlooking the lake and the expensive little theater of Via Serlas, where the international winter set gathers each year to perform its familiar rituals of consumption.

Inside, the atmosphere is grand hotel in the fullest, least apologetic sense: chandeliers, imposing public rooms, formal service, and interiors that understand the importance of making an entrance. The original rooms remain reassuringly traditional, and the lake-facing ones are the ones worth asking for (Hitchcock, for his part, kept Suite 501). The Serlas Wing, opened in 2025, offers a contemporary counterpoint, its 25 rooms and suites by Antonio Citterio and Patricia Viel finished in local stone, oak, and Loro Piana Interiors wool. A three-minute walk from the property leads to Chesa Veglia, a 17th-century farmhouse housing several restaurants and bars, including beloved favorites, like Pizzeria Heuboden, the Carigiet Fondue Stübli and the Polo Bar, among others.

Back in the Palace, Matsuhisa occupies what was once Switzerland’s first indoor tennis hall, which is set to debut a reimagined design this winter by Martin Brudnizki Design Studio, while a new bar designed by Milanese designer Giuseppe Porcelli will welcome guests in Le Grand Hall. Up on Corviglia, Paradiso, the hotel’s mountain restaurant, trades chandeliers for panoramic views, Alpine fare, and a livelier après-ski scene. The Renaissance Bar is where the evening tends to end, preferably with a whisky, a cigar, and a seat by the fire. The spa’s glass-walled infinity pool looks straight out at the lake; even the business of doing very little ought to come with a view.

Amenities: Spa, restaurants, bars, pool, shuttle, on-site ski rental

Founded by Johannes Badrutt in 1856, the Kulm helped establish St. Moritz as a winter resort. Set above the village with sweeping views across the Engadin, the hotel balances its sporting heritage with a distinctly contemporary appetite for reinvention. Many of its 150 rooms and suites have been refreshed by Pierre-Yves Rochon, while the restaurants range from Amaru, Claudia Canessa’s Peruvian-inspired restaurant dressed in contemporary whimsy by Luke Edward Hall, to Mauro Colagreco’s Kulm Country Club, housed in a neighboring building with its own ice rink. Sunny Bar, a St. Moritz institution in its own right, remains essential for a drink and a dose of local history.

The latest addition is the Alpine Sports Lounge & Boutique, designed by Foster + Partners for winter 2025. Clad in fragrant Swiss stone pine, it reimagines the conventional ski room with private fitting areas, specialist equipment, a ski concierge, and a pantry serving healthy snacks and energy shots. The idea is to get guests from suite to slope with rather less fuss, and considerably more style.

Amenities: Restaurants, bars, ice rink, shuttle, on-site ski rental

Few hotels have so thoroughly shaped the identity of the place they inhabit as Gstaad Palace has shaped that of Gstaad itself. Rising above the village like a white castle, it belongs to an older conception of luxury, when glamour required a little grandeur and there was an art to knowing exactly who was in the room (and that they may prefer not to announce themselves). Behind its turreted façade are ninety rooms and suites, five restaurants, a sprawling spa, indoor and outdoor pools, and the GreenGo, the legendary nightclub that has entertained generations of international society. Its corridors have absorbed the passing of royalty, financiers, and film stars.

One comes here, presumably, for the mountains, the service, and the fondue that’s served in a former wartime bunker. But one also comes for the sense of entering a world that has long since ceased to exist anywhere else—except, somehow, on this hill above Gstaad, where the old rituals of privilege continue to be performed with magnificent, almost theatrical conviction.

Amenities: Restaurants, spa, shuttle, on-site ski rental

Gstaad has always done luxury in a particular, old-money key, and The Alpina carries that tradition forward with a more contemporary hand. The 55 rooms are fitted with carved ceilings, timber walls and Swiss farmhouse cupboards, and even the leather straps once used to hang cowbells turn up as decoration. Meanwhile, above the main staircase is a hand-painted ceiling made in southern Europe around 1780 and painstakingly restored. New executive chef Francesco De Bartolomeis oversees the hotel’s entire food offering, so dinner can be Japanese at Megu or Bernese at the Swiss Stübli, with a cellar of 1,700-plus labels behind either. It isn’t ski-in, ski-out, but a shuttle runs to the lifts and the hotel sorts passes and rentals. The Six Senses Spa is vast, and its menu runs from Tibetan healing to bio-hacking therapies, such as their hyperbaric oxygen chamber.

Amenities: Restaurants, spa, shuttle, on-site ski rental

Suvretta House occupies a rather different corner of the St. Moritz universe. Opened in 1912, it sits away from the village center, surrounded by mountain scenery and woodland, in a position that feels deliberately removed from the main procession of boutiques, champagne bars, and other seasonal distractions. Its fairytale exterior and grand interiors are unapologetically old-world, retaining the grandeur and traditions of the great Alpine hotels, but with a more secluded, sporting character. This is a hotel for people who regard a ski holiday as something that ought to involve actual skiing: It has direct ski-in/ski-out access to the Corviglia slopes, its own ski facilities, and a long-standing connection to the mountain that sets it apart from properties in the village.

For lunch on the slopes, there’s Trutz, near the top of the Suvretta lift, while Chasellas, down at the base, is the place to stop for a hot chocolate after skiing. Back at the hotel, the Grand Restaurant offers an altogether more formal expression of Alpine luxury, with elaborate interiors, traditional service and a culinary repertoire that combines French influences with international touches. Among its most famous dishes is spaghetti with caviar, a luxurious yet understated signature that reflects the Grand Restaurant’s timeless elegance. Afternoon tea and a swim in the pool within the hotel’s expansive, freshly renovated spa complete the experience. Suvretta’s particular appeal lies in this combination of grandeur, sporting heritage, and seclusion… with a hotel shuttle to bring you into town in a matter of minutes whenever you’re ready to rejoin the scene.

Amenities: Spa, restaurants, pool, ski-in, ski-out, shuttle, on-site ski rental

Address: Via Chasellas 1, 7500 St. Moritz

#6699. Taco Bell Is Expanding Its Cantina Menu With Six New Steak Creations

Your usual order could be getting some serious competition.

Taste-testing Taco Bell's new FLAMIN' HOT menu items should've bought my stomach at least a few days off. Instead, the chain has already given me another reason to start thinking about my next order.

Taco Bell is testing a new carne asada protein across six menu items, giving its Cantina lineup another round of additions. But of course, there's a catch. As of November 12, it's only available in Nashville, Tennessee, and the Minneapolis-St. Paul area. So if you're lucky enough to live in either market, congratulations. I'll just be over here drooling over the pictures.

The steak itself sounds pretty different from what Taco Bell currently serves. It gets a marinade with citrus and savory seasonings before being cooked sous vide, then seared and cut into small chunks. Taco Bell says it's going for a deeper, more grilled flavor, and rather than giving it one or two menu appearances, the chain has come up with six ways to try it.

The Cantina Carne Asada Chalupa Lime Bowl is probably the most loaded of the bunch, piling steak, rice, black beans, guacamole, pico de gallo, cheese, and purple cabbage slaw together with chile-lime seasoned Chalupa Chips. There's also a Cantina Carne Asada Burrito, which wraps the meat in a new Sonoran-style flour tortilla with lettuce, cabbage, cheese, pico, and Spicy Ranch Sauce before getting grilled.

If tacos are more your speed, there are three options. The Cantina Carne Asada Crispy Taco comes in a fried corn shell with cheese grilled onto the outside, while the Cantina Carne Asada Soft Taco uses that same new flour tortilla with cabbage slaw and Spicy Ranch. Then there's the smaller Cantina Carne Asada Street Chalupa, which has a fried shell lined with crispy cheese.

Rounding things out is the Cantina Carne Asada Rolled Quesadilla, stuffed with steak, a three-cheese blend, and Spicy Ranch before being grilled and sliced. All six items also come with an Avocado Verde Salsa packet.

The rollout follows Taco Bell's push to give its Cantina menu more attention, including the slow-roasted chicken that's already made its way into items like the Cantina Chicken Mexican Pizza. This latest test could eventually put carne asada on the permanent menu, although there's no word yet on whether it'll expand beyond those two markets.

#6697. Robert Pattinson, I’m Begging You For a Quirked-Up James Bond

Our long international nightmare is finally over: two-time Meme of the Year nominee Robert Pattinson has been chosen as Daniel Craig’s James Bond successor, bringing an end to an exhausting series of “reports” and “leaks” about Amazon’s search for a new 007. Finally we can stop the debates and fan-casting and let Patts and Denis Villeneuve cook until they’re ready to present their new vision. But that would require a level of restraint that the internet doesn’t typically exercise. Immediately after the protracted process of casting Bond concluded, the internet moved on to naming its dream picks for Bond Girls and Bond Villains (sometimes, to brilliant effect.) I can’t say I have a dog in either fight, at least not right now. My Bond WishList is of a different magnitude altogether: can we make James Bond silly again? Just a little, even, 15 percent goofball?

In the hands of another (read: more limited) actor, I’d never suggest such a risky swerve. But the best thing about Pattinson is his range. Sure, if Villeneuve and co. want to render Bond as the stoic and taciturn gentleman he’s generally been this century, Rob has proven he can do that, as every Tenet truther has been gleefully preaching for the last 24 hours. But more often than not, Pattinson is keen to get weird, whether that’s going Full Freak, as he does in Primetime, or approaching certain archetypal parts with a silly, goofy mood (like his conniving suitor in The Odyssey). He can do a “voice” (Mickey 17), he can do scumbag grime (Good Time), he can do hapless screwball (The Drama). Why not make what’ll be his biggest role to date a little cocktail of all his best elements? (Okay, he can leave the Mickey 17 voice behind.)

20 years ago, Casino Royale was a refreshing reset and a crucial corrective to the overflowing ridiculousness of the Piece Brosnan era. But in the past two decades, the pendulum has swung back—the gritty reboot has become studios' stock-in-trade. I feel the same way about Batman; the actual risky choice would be to make something less like Nolan’s series that, instead, hewed a little closer to, say, Batman Forever, or even the gothic camp of Tim Burton’s two films.

Of course, Robert Pattinson was at the center of a Batman reboot as well, and the result was a movie that felt more like a spiritual cousin to David Fincher’s Se7en; audiences ate it up so much that the hunger for a sequel persists even after endless delays. When it comes to franchises as high-stakes as Batman or Bond, you can’t trust these increasingly sauceless execs to make anything but the basic choice. There’s no reason to expect Jeff Bezos isn’t texting Denis screenshots from Skyfall for reference from his megayacht at this very moment.

But if there’s anybody capable of putting a little English on the handle while still giving the mainstream what it wants, it’s Big Bob Pattinson. He could easily make his James Bond a little off, or he could go full seductive cad who smiles like Neil Tenet, has a ki with Q, and charms women with some playful banter instead of simply brooding them into submission. I’m not looking for invisible cars and sharks with lasers, or a Lothario like Roger Moore who speaks in puns. All I’m asking is that we give camp a chance. Because ultimately, the most exciting thing Villeneuve and Pattinson can do to set their Bond apart would be to loosen him up a little.

#6696. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6694. Vogue France Head of Editorial Content Claire Thomson-Jonville’s Guide to Megève

To be sure, there’s no shortage of quaint, storybook villages in any part of the Alps—but over on the French side, tucked away in the Haute-Savoie region, there’s something special about Megève. “I’ve been coming for years; I enjoy it just as much in summer as in winter,” says Vogue France’s Head of Editorial Content, Claire Thomson-Jonville. “I love that it still feels like a small, cozy village. It’s postcard-perfect with a family-friendly atmosphere; it’s discreet, not flashy, with incredible nature.”

While the hiking—and generally stunning landscape—is a great draw for year-round tourism, travelers in the winter really have one reason to visit: the skiing. Thomson-Jonville has her routine down: “One of my favorite things to do is to take a moniteur de ski for the day and head into the mountains, around Mont d’Arbois.” (On her more adventurous days, she’ll brave the challenging pistes a little farther out at Mont Blanc.) In between stints on the slopes, she’s developed a list of local favorites, for everything from designer fashion to where you can find the best raclette; ahead, she offers us a peek into her Megève address book.

For a one-of-a-kind clothing find: Allard is a classic—a Megève institution. It’s on the square beside the church, the maison behind the original ski fuseau created in the 1930s. It’s a lovely place to find a beautiful sweater. Blu&Berry is where I go to find something more unexpected; they have pieces from The Row and Celine. Big Boss is another Megève institution, with a great skiwear selection. It’s one of those shops that everyone who comes here regularly knows.

For a worthwhile investment piece: The Hermès store in Megève is particularly well-stocked, and the Loro Piana boutique in the center of the village is great for après-ski shopping!

For unique souvenirs: Again, Allard for something classic that feels connected to the village. For something more unusual, there’s Max et Isa; it’s great for antique jewelry, vintage Murano lamps, and decorative objects. It’s a good address to browse for an unusual gift or a special piece for your chalet.

For the magpie: Guilhem Joaillier is my favorite jewelry store in Megève. I’ve picked some meaningful pieces here over the years; it’s a solid gift shop, too. Someone always has a birthday when we’re in Megève, and, of course, there’s always Christmas.

For your next great read: Scarlett Megève has a good curation of art books, as well as fun decorative objects. It’s a good place to buy gifts. The Maison de La Presse in town is the place we all go to buy magazines and novels; it’s super simple but you’ll always bump into someone you know there. Megève is a small place!

For the quickest way to impress an out-of-towner: I spend a lot of time in the Pharmacie de la Tour on Place de l’Église—it’s full of little treasures. I love an après-ski French pharmacy haul. Vitamins, moisturizers, supplements, hair masks… I love trying out new products when I’m in the mountains.

For a pick-me-up treat: Le Hibou Blanc is a great address for brunch or a coffee. It’s in the center of town with a big, heated terrasse to sit outside with a cappuccino and watch the world go by.

For a luxurious lunch: L’Idéal 1850, up on Mont d’Arbois, for a lunch break between runs with a beautiful mountain view. It’s very social; wear a great ski outfit the day you book a table.

For a fabulous dinner reservation: I love Le Vieux Megève. It’s a cheerful, traditional spot in the village—it’s noisy, yummy, and so much fun. Book early to share a raclette or fondue with family or friends. It’s my favorite spot in Megève—in fact, everyone in my family loves it there. It’s a unanimous favorite.

For a different kind of evening, I love Kaito at the Four Seasons. The sushi is delicious, and it’s a bit of a scene. Dress up and people watch!

For a post-slope spa day: I always love to try new places, but to me, Les Fermes de Marie has the best spa in Megève. The facials are great. The Susanne Kaufmann spa at Les Chalets du Mont d’Arbois is also good for bodywork.

For an apéro.. or a nightcap: The bar at the Fer à Cheval. It’s cozy and welcoming—a perfect place to settle by the fire after a day in the mountains, plus it’s in the center of town. The bar at the Four Seasons after dinner is also a vibe for the people watching.

For your packing list: My mountain packing list is tried and tested: One ski look, one puffy ski jacket, a (fake) fur coat, cashmere joggers, and big sunglasses. I also pack UGGs and cashmere socks for warmth, plus some great earrings to liven up a low-key dinner look.
