#6675. The Fearless Sensitivity of ‘Mouse’ and ‘Clarissa’ Star Sophie Okonedo

Sophie Okonedo is one of those performers whose very presence can make a scene feel more alive. The Tony Award–winning British actor projects both warmth and watchfulness, moving swiftly from humor to hurt, or authority to vulnerability, without announcing the shift. Even in a supporting role, she has a way of making you lean in.

This winter she leads two independent features opening theatrically after an international festival run: Clarissa, by brothers Chuko and Arie Esiri, and Mouse, by husband-and-wife team Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson. Though shot nearly a year apart, the two films are arriving within weeks of each other—a quirk of the release calendar that makes for an unusually timely double feature.

Mouse, out now, is a coming-of-age story set in 2002 Arkansas, in which the teenage Minnie (Katherine Mallen Kupferer) develops a complicated relationship with her best friend’s mother (Okonedo) after an unexpected tragedy. Meanwhile, Clarissa—in limited theaters December 18—transposes Virginia Woolf’s novel Mrs. Dalloway to contemporary Nigeria, a project that brought Okonedo to a country she hadn’t visited in two decades. (Her late father, whom she was mostly estranged from, moved back to his home country when she was young.)

Filming in Lagos proved consequential in ways that extended well beyond the work itself. “The journey I had in Lagos was so immense, personally and professionally, that I remember thinking on the wrap day that even if nothing else happens with this film, I’ve already gotten everything I wanted,” she tells Vogue.

Both films were made on tiny budgets, and as Okonedo points out, a conversation about one inevitably opens up a conversation about the other. So we talked about both.

Vogue: Let’s start with Mouse. How did it come to you? What was it about your character, Helen, or about the directors that made you say yes?

Sophie Okonedo: I didn’t read anything about them. I read the script completely cold. By the time I got to the end, I rang my agent and said, “I’m absolutely doing this. I don’t know who’s directing, I don’t know what’s happening with the film, but I’m doing it.” So he sent me their last film, Ghostlight. It’s such a brilliant film, and it was made for pennies. These are two really interesting filmmakers who are talking about America in a way I haven’t seen—very quietly. There are no explosions, no big movie stars, and it’s deeply significant. Kelly’s writing is subtle and real. But films like this can slip by without anyone noticing. I have to galvanize everyone and get them behind it because I think it’s so good.

Helen ends up mothering her daughter’s friend, Minnie, in a way that’s unnerving at times, as if she’s grieving and replacing her at the same time.

It’s totally inappropriate at times. She even says it at one point: “Oh my God, I’m the adult here.” She uses Minnie to ease her own grief, then backtracks, then moves forward again. It’s a messy situation, but there’s hope in it. The film is funny too. Kelly has that gift for finding levity in dark situations. But they never get you to play the comedy. You play the seriousness of it all, and it’s funny as it goes along.

I realized after watching the film that the woman playing Katherine’s mother is her real-life mother. What was that dynamic like on set?

She wasn’t even meant to play the part at first. Tara [Mallen], her mother, is a theater actress. She runs a theater company in Chicago and was there as Katherine’s guardian. They’d cast a great local actor, but on the first day we realized it wasn’t right. By the second day, Tara stepped in. Everything was so homegrown. My baby in the film is actually Kelly and Alex’s baby. They removed all the blockers you normally have as an actor on a film, where you spend three hours in hair and makeup. Sometimes you need those things, but this film didn’t. You just rock up and start filming. It was very seamless.

Katherine Mallen Kupferer and Sophie Okonedo in Mouse

You shot on location in North Little Rock. Had you been to Arkansas before?

Never. I got there a little early to check it out because I was playing an outsider but an outsider who’d lived there for 15 years. So I had to know the place and feel familiar with it. All the locations came from [O’Sullivan’s] childhood. You could ask her, “What happened here?” and she’d tell you. Many people with small parts in the film knew Kelly from high school and were now playing mothers. The dance we see at the memorial was one Kelly actually performed herself. We even brought back the dance teacher who taught her so she could teach it to the two girls in the film.

Does playing an outsider give you something to work with? You didn’t do the method thing, keeping yourself apart from everyone, right?

No. I totally get that some people do, but I’m too shy to stay in character! I feel too silly. What I do is think very deeply about every single word I say in the script before I arrive. Because I’m theater trained, the script is my bible. All answers will be there. I spend a long time thinking about everything I say and everything everyone else says, and I go through it many, many times. An internal world builds up inside me. I can’t really explain how it happens. When I get to set, I forget any notes or journals I’ve made. I drop it all, empty myself, and see what happens. I feel buoyant and flexible, not stuck in any particular way.

Mouse is so specific about 2002, down to the Michelle Branch music cues. I was a bit younger than the characters then, but it all felt right. What did setting it in that moment bring to the story?

I’m older, but Kelly was that age in 2002, so she had all the references. She knew exactly what she was listening to, what she was thinking and feeling. The main difference is there were no cell phones back then. If you wanted information, it had to come to you through someone taking action. The jogger has to tell Minnie something, then she has to run to the house to see if it’s really happened, then she has to look for a phone book. Now it would just be someone posting “RIP Callie” on Instagram. It’s so much more interesting to film people taking an action than all these constant shots of phones and texts, which I see in movies all the time now. It’s so boring.

In Mouse, Helen and Minnie come from very different backgrounds. Class is also woven into Clarissa, where you play the titular role. Was that a connection you were conscious of while working on the two films?

Class is massive in Britain. We live and breathe it. It runs through every vein of everyone’s body here, probably more than anything else, so I’m very aware of it. But there’s another weird parallel between the films: Mouse is directed by a couple, and one of them is the writer. Clarissa is directed by two brothers, and one of them is the writer. With both, I had an instant, visceral response. I didn’t need to think about the whys and wherefores. It was just yes, yes, yes. With a lot of other work, I have to get myself into the right position or work it out. What’s also amazing is that the scripts for Clarissa and Mouse barely changed between that first draft and the start of filming—the same was true of Janet Planet. These are filmmakers who have thought deeply about what they’re writing. There weren’t a million drafts or endless revisions; all three films were already in a remarkably evolved state from the start. Even though Mouse looks improvised in places, I’m sticking to the script.

But parts of Mouse were improvised, right? I’m thinking of the scene where Helen attends a grief group.

It was a real grief group. I knew the man handing me coffee at the beginning was an actor, though by coincidence he was also in a grief group. I was just outside the room; they put two cameras in there, and someone called action. I walked in, and during the scene it slowly dawned on me—someone had forgotten to tell me these weren’t actors!

The scene is short, but that take lasted an hour and 10 minutes—the exact length of the group. If it were scripted, I probably would have talked and broken down. But I couldn’t speak; their stories were so extraordinary. I kept talking to them afterward, thinking the cameras had stopped, until I realized they were still filming. Alex will do that. You don’t even know. There’s no “cut.”

Both films are concerned with motherhood, though in very different ways. In Mouse, there’s an absent daughter; in Clarissa, she keeps her living daughter at arm’s length. Did these characters speak to each other in any way?

It’s a good question, because I find that when I do a part, it usually feeds into the next one. The next role I played after Clarissa was Natalya in Turgenev’s A Month in the Country, in London. She’s a woman of a certain age looking back, wondering whether she made the right choices, and she has a very separate relationship with her son. I was thinking that a lot of Clarissa was in her.

I read that Arie and Chuko drew on their own mother in shaping the film and that you got to spend time with her. How did that influence your performance?

When they cast me, I wondered if I could do this. I told them I didn’t recognize the Lagos in the script and that I had such a fractured relationship with the country. They said, “If nothing else, we’ll bridge that for you.” That meant a lot. Before filming, Chuko invited me to stay with him and his mother. I ended up staying the whole shoot and got very close to her. I used her a lot, more than she realizes, perhaps. Like Clarissa, she employs staff [in her home], and I observed how she interacted with them. I didn’t want to turn her into a caricature out of Downton Abbey. You can just be real with them, the way she was.

You also just don’t see stories like this coming out of Africa, and I say that broadly. The subject matter is usually very narrow: Africa is depicted as war-torn, impoverished. Here was a film about people. There’s a backdrop of war and social and economic circumstances, but that isn’t the main thrust. I long to see films where we as Africans, as Nigerians, get every part of ourselves represented, just as our white Western counterparts get films about everything. It’s the same with queer films and Black films: They shouldn’t only be about being queer or Black. That shouldn’t have to be the whole story.

And on top of that, Clarissa is character driven and not plot driven.

The thought of going to Lagos and making an arthouse film on 35 millimeter was incredible. It’s an impossible book to film. People have tried many times, and mostly it doesn’t work. I was taking a punt. I just wanted to be part of it. I hardly say anything but say a million words with my face.

What is it like to project that kind of interiority? It’s sort of a paradox: Clarissa is deep in thought, but she also doesn’t let you in much.

She’s hard to read, but you have to make her really easy to read for the camera. She’s protective, but you have to let the camera in. I didn’t think about it that deeply. I just have that sort of face. I’m really sensitive, hypersensitive, which is so difficult in my normal life, but it’s great for acting. My grandmother used to say, “Your face changes like the wind.” Everything shows. Chuko or Arie would only have to whisper the slightest thing in my ear, and it would show.

People always say to watch an actor’s eyes, but I noticed so much happens in the lower half of your face. It holds everything.

That’s why I could never do any of that stuff to my face. I’d be too frightened! I know I only have to think the glimmer of a thought and it’ll show. I don’t know what happens to my face because I don’t really watch myself, but doing something that would stop that would be the end of my career.

The story famously centers on your character throwing a party. Are you more of a host or a guest?

I’m quite a good host, actually. I don’t do it often because I go overboard and it’s exhausting. I love cooking and making lovely things. I used to spend the whole time panicking in the kitchen, but I’ve learned it doesn’t really matter what you serve. It’s about how you engage with guests. They just want you to be part of the party.

Did you watch any of the other adaptations of Mrs. Dalloway to prepare for Clarissa?

I watched about three minutes of one with Vanessa Redgrave and realized we’re not doing this type of film, so I didn’t carry on. Chuko and Arie would have watched everything, though. They’re complete cinephiles.

Did they give you suggestions on films to watch to prepare then?

They probably did, but I forgot because my brain is a sieve. They gave up on me. They’d mention really famous films, and I’d say I hadn’t seen them. I don’t know what I do with my time. I don’t fill it wisely. I just seem to mess around most of the day, and then it’s gone!

It sounds like you’re living your own stories instead of watching other people’s on screen.

You’re putting it nicely. As my husband says, I spend a lot of time daydreaming. I’ve got a really nice view. [Turns her laptop to the window to show the view.] I spend a lot of time just looking out at the trees with my dog.

After this double-header year, what are you looking for next?

Because I’m getting older, I don’t see an eternity stretching out in front of me anymore, and I find myself asking how I want to spend my time. I’ve decided that my heart is really in independent films and theater, so I’m going to wait until the right thing comes along. You might find me still unemployed a year from now. Nothing has come up yet that’s been worth getting on a plane for.

This conversation has been edited and condensed.

#6674. Your Exclusive First Look at the Official 'Cameron Winter at Carnegie' Hall Merch

“I will keep rolling down until my best shirt rolls off,” warbles Cameron Winter on “The Rolling Stone,” the opening track of his 2024 solo debut Heavy Metal. That album later became the basis of the Geese frontman’s historic December 2025 performance at Carnegie Hall, which was filmed and subsequently turned into a captivating concert film by Oscar-winning director Paul Thomas Anderson. A year later, Winter—and perhaps you—will now have a new best shirt to roll off.

PTA’s Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall, which was shot on 35mm and 16mm film, will hit select theaters nationwide on Friday. As a reward to the Geeseheads and steadfast cinephiles who attend the 35mm screenings, distributor Janus Films produced a limited-edition run of merch (many such cases!) that can only be purchased IRL at select participating theaters. Which is to say, acquiring this merch…takes miles.

But if you’re looking at the Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall T-shirts ($40) and baseball hats ($35) and thinking, “Wow, those look a lot like the maximalist, erudite wares from Boot Boyz Biz,” that’s because they were in fact designed by two of the Chicago brand’s current outposts, Now-Time and Mike’s Deli.

In an email, the Now-Time/Mike’s Deli team said that they drew inspiration from Carnegie Hall’s history and architecture. “We looked to the building itself as a visual archive to draw from, seeking forms that resonated with the performance across time,” they wrote. “Familiar architectural details took on a new heightened significance, knowing what was happening inside. In Carnegie Hall’s classic horseshoe layout we saw the camera’s panoramic intent. Outside on the 19th-century facade we found typographic elements that paralleled the energy of the event.” A very Winteresque explanation, in a way. Ideal for any enigmatic T-shirt enthusiast.

If you, too, would like to participate in the seeking forms and panoramic intent of Winter’s moving piano stylings on one winter’s night in Manhattan, you better start a-walking to the nearest 35mm-equipped cinema near you.

#6673. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6672. Harry Styles-Approved Designer Macy Grimshaw Just Won the 2026 H&M Design Award

Her off-kilter pieces have also been worn by Emma Corrin, Simone Ashley, and Anya Taylor-Joy.

Earlier this year, Macy Grimshaw presented her graduate collection from Central Saint Martins at London Fashion Week, styled by Harry Lambert, the mind behind the wardrobes of Emma Corrin, Alexander Skarsgård, and Harry Styles. Since then, the 25-year-old designer has continued to rise, dressing the likes of Anya Taylor-Joy, Simone Ashley, and several of Lambert’s clients—Corrin and Styles among them—in her semi-surrealist separates and top-notch leatherwork. Now, Grimshaw has a major accolade to cap off her standout year: the 2026 H&M Design Award.

At the presentation on Wednesday afternoon in London, Grimshaw was chosen among seven other finalists from top design universities across the globe: Chico Yu, Ennis Finnerty Mackay, Evelina Kryvopust, Fantin Delattre Pirenne, Jessica Lin, Macy Grimshaw, Yichun Liu, and Yvonne Schichtel. Grimshaw will receive a €150,000 ($164,655) endowment, a yearlong mentorship, and will have her collection produced and sold in selected H&M stores worldwide and online in October 2027. Each finalist was awarded a €10,000 ($10,980) endowment.

“She left me with desire and intrigue to see how she can actually develop the work,” said Beka Gvishiani, founder of Style Not Com, who joined H&M’s creative advisor Ann-Sofie Johansson, model Paloma Elsesser, and designer Ib Kamara on the jury. “For the moment, it’s very much the artist’s work,” he continued. “But she has ideas about how to make it wearable for daywear, because some of the pieces are great for an event or a performance.”

Gvishiani highlights the collection’s more experimental pieces, like a rusted, laser-cut mesh minidress ornamented with padlocks or a terracotta-hued molded bustier scattered with discarded cigarette butts. The scenography of the latter was inspired, naturally, by the brick wall where CSM students gather on smoke breaks.

But in between those more experimental moments, it’s easy to see why Grimshaw walked away with the prize, H&M’s first time awarding it since 2020. While fodder for celebrity placements and red carpets, her work also carries “hanger appeal,” clothes that are both wearable and appealing but also evoke something unexpected and slightly “off.” Like a texturized, scalloped suit jacket with a taut waist à la the “New Look” or the almost wet-looking crumpled silk slip dress done in a graphic, almost watercolor effect.

The line took cues from the designer’s college years in London (at 18, she moved there from Hong Kong to attend CSM) and speaks to her introspective way of working. “My whole practice is inspired by my grandmother having Alzheimer’s and trying to represent the fading of memories by using everyday objects and to recontextualize them,” Grimshaw told ELLE after the award was announced. “I want to remind us not to take the everyday for granted; that’s why a lot of my work is pencil shavings, cigarettes, locks.”

Next up, the designer will head to H&M’s home base of Stockholm, where she’ll get started on her collaboration with the brand. “This opportunity is going to be a massive help to make my work accessible to everyone,” she adds. “I’m very excited because this collection was not designed with the idea of commerciality. So I’m really interested to challenge myself and also work with other people to see how it can become that.”

#6671. French Onion Croissant Strata

A breakfast strata is one of our go-tos when we want a hearty, shareable brunch dish, but it’s hard to put into words how good this French onion croissant strata is. It takes a few extra minutes to deeply caramelize the onions, but the extra flavor and richness make a HUGE difference.

Making it French Onion:Caramelizing the onions over medium heat helps them brown evenly and consistently. If the onions begin to stick or burn, add a splash of water to bring them back! Garlic, thyme, and black pepper are the aromatic unsung heroes in the onions, so you don’t want to skip them. Deglazing with white wine is essential in any French onion recipe, so use the one you’d sip! Once the wine has reduced, add some beef stock to impart meaty French onion soup flavor. The caramelized onions then get layered with torn croissants and Gruyère cheese, and topped with dollops of cream cheese.

Delish Official:Eggland's Best Eggs are the Official Eggs of Delish. That means they're the only eggs we're using in our recipe content.

Storage:The beautiful thing about a breakfast strata is that you can make it ahead. Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 day and reheat until the internal temperature reaches 165°. This is also great to portion and store for breakfast at the office.

#6670. Stylist and Creative Director Akari Endo-Gaut’s Guide to Tokyo

Perhaps no city juggles the past and the future as nimbly as Tokyo. Sleek skyscrapers meet centuries-old shrines; a rich culinary tradition blends with contemporary innovation (it’s no accident that this is the city with the most Michelin starred-restaurants in the world). The fashion, of course, exists in a similar dichotomy, expertly blending traditional techniques with the avant-garde. There’s never a wrong time to visit the Japanese capital—but in winter, when ski resorts a quick day trip away are in full swing and New Year’s celebrations are on the horizon, it feels particularly special. All you have to do is narrow down your itinerary.

In fact, there’s so much to discover that you could spend an entire trip dedicated to shopping alone—according to Akari Endo-Gaut, a Japan-born, New York-based stylist and creative director who studied in Tokyo, it may be worth bringing a second suitcase just for souvenirs. From the vintage shops to put on your radar to the best place to stop for a glass of natural wine, here’s a glimpse at Endo-Gaut’s Tokyo little black book.

For a one-of-a-kind clothing find: Since I was student in Tokyo, one of my favorite areas to hang around was Minami-Aoyama. We used to have amazing Corso Como store there; now, the Comme des Garçons store, the Issey Miyake Pleats Please shop, and the Auralee store there are still where you can go to find a special piece.

For vintage gems: There are so many good vintage shops in Tokyo, and it goes deep. BerBer Jin is always my first stop, and I also check luxury resale shops like Komehyo.

For unique souvenirs: You can find the best curated products, from ceramic bowls to German knives, at Arts and Science. And beautifully wrapped sweets at Higashiya are the best gifts.

For a worthwhile investment piece: Wako Arts and Culture is a new space conceived by artist Hiroshi Sugimoto in the basement of a prestigious department store in Ginza. It’s all specially curated, a great spot to find a special piece from fashion to Japanese craft.

For the magpie: My very talented friend Charlotte Chesnais from Paris recently opened a shop in Tokyo; it’s a must-visit. Or, if you’re looking for best-condition vintage watches, you can go to ECW Shoto.

For your next great read: Japan has a big book culture—go to Komiyama bookstore for vintage books, or spend a full weekend browsing at Tsutaya Daikanyama or SKAC.

For stylish home goods: You can find traditional but beautiful kitchen goods at Kiya and, of course, at Muji. Or, spend a fun day exploring all the kitchen goods stores in the Kappabashi area, which is a shopping street dedicated to restaurant owners.

For the quickest way to impress an out-of-towner: Hakujitsu houses a beautiful collection of ceramics in an old dentist building. My secret favorite is Yanaka Matsunoya—it has the best baskets and tote bags.

For a fabulous dinner reservation: I love Japanese-Chinese food or yakiniku, so I go to Chugoku Hanten with local friends or to Jojoen with my sister. If I have foreign guests, they usually have fun dining experience at Narukiyo.

For a bakery treat: Sawamura is our best local bakery cafe in Hiroo. After a soba lunch at Kanda, stop by Omiya Western Sweets Shop for the cutest pastry; for traditional Japanese sweets at an upscale, architecturally beautiful spot, go to Toraya Akasaka.

For the art-lover: Taka Ishii and Tomio Koyama are the best fine arts galleries in Tokyo. I like the artists from Kosaku Kanechika too, and at Licht gallery, you can see the best design pieces.

For an apéro.. or a nightcap: For the architecture lover, a drink at Imperial Bar, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright, is a must. When I’m hanging out with local friends, I’d go for a natural wine at Le Cabaret or Tabac.

For your packing list: Honestly, you don’t need anything, since you go to Tokyo to buy the best of all items! Bring flat shoes for walking, and an extra suitcase for shopping. An eye mask and melatonin for the 13-hour time difference will come in handy, as will a handkerchief; it’s part of local etiquette to carry one. And I always like to bring a running outfit for the famous Imperial Palace run.

#6669. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6667. Noah Wrapped the Converse Chuck 70 in Menswear’s Favorite Tartan

When Converse and Noah collaborated for the first time earlier this year, the most surprising thing was that it’d taken so long for them to link up. The sneaker OGs and New York menswear mavens make as much sense together as peanut butter and jelly—both brands flow effortlessly between worlds, embraced by punks and preps and hoopers and skaters alike. Thankfully, the duo have been making up for lost time, kicking their partnership off with a couple of killer Chuck 70s in the spring before putting out an understated banger of a spin on the Louie Lopez 2 over the summer. Now, they’re capping off their banner year with one last go-round—another jazzed-up Chuck Taylor that’s about as holiday-ready as it gets.

Just in time for turkey season, Noah has wrapped the Converse Chuck 70 Low in one of the most beloved patterns in menswear: Black Watch tartan. The green, navy, and black plaid was originally worn by squadrons patrolling the Scottish Highlands in the 18th century, with its subdued tones meant to help wearers blend into their surroundings. Over the past several decades, it’s been embraced by fashion at large, but particularly Trad Ivy enthusiasts, who tend to sport the striking tartan on everything from sport coats and scarves during the colder months.

In addition to the sharp Black Watch canvas uppers, Noah made a handful of other subtle changes to the classic silhouette, adding its branding to the “license plate” on the shoe’s heel, removing the wing tongue stitch, and swapping in a woven tongue tag. The kicks feature the standard white laces but also come with a mustard yellow pair for an extra boost of color.

If you’re looking to dress festively but aren’t all that into freaky patterned sweaters, the latest Converse x Noah Chuck 70 Low might just be the ticket. The shoes drop tomorrow, November 19, for $112 via both Converse and Noah.

#6666. Homemade Mac & Cheese

The perfect mac & cheese will have you dreaming about its cheesy goodness for days after you eat it. Obviously, the cheese has to be top-notch, but the real secret to the best version is the perfect crunchy topping. My recipe delivers on all of that and more, so you won't even think about reaching for another mac & cheese recipe for the rest of your gatherings. From weeknight dinners to potlucks and holidays, this is the classic side dish everyone will be reaching for.

What People Are Saying:"Always a huge hit with friends and family! This is my go-to if I'm bringing a dish to a holiday dinner with friends. I've rarely had leftovers to take home!" - Zafire_Shadows

"This is exactly what mac and cheese dreams are made of. Love the gruyere funk and the mustard powder (so clever!)." - Pastagofer

First, you’ll boil the pasta. Start with a big pot of salted water (and I mean super salty, it should taste like the ocean), then add your pasta and cook it until before al dente—I’m talking still-has-a-ring-of-hard-white-pasta-in-the-middle-when-you-bite-in uncooked. You want it to meld and absorb with your cheese sauce in the oven, not turn into mush. Undercooking now guarantees the perfect bite when you pull it out of the oven.

Then it’s cheese sauce time, and that means making a béchamel. You’ll start by melting your butter in a pan over medium heat, then sprinkling the flour over the top and stirring everything together until it starts pulling away from the pan slightly. You’re looking for what’s called a “blonde roux,” which has a slightly yellow tint and should smell a bit like baked goods. You don’t want it super dark (so keep an eye on the heat!), but you definitely don’t want it as light as it started.

Next, add the milk in slowly, stirring constantly so you don’t get thick lumps. Want to shortcut this process a bit? Heat your milk ahead of time to room temperature or even slightly warm. You’re going to cook it until it’s thick and bubbly (about 2 minutes), so having your milk warm will help you get there faster. It’s going to get a LOT thicker when you add the cheese, so if it’s still a little thin but you want to get on with it, that’s okay too.

Once you’re ready to add the cheese, it’s very important to take it off the heat before so that the sauce doesn’t start to separate. That said, if you’ve been at it for a minute and are still having trouble getting your cheese to melt, pop your pot back on the heat for just a few seconds to bring the temperature up and help the process along.

Once it comes together, you can stir in the macaroni until every noodle is coated.

At this point, you could eat this mac & cheese right now, and it would taste wonderful. But! If you want exceptional mac & cheese, you’ve gotta bake it. So pour it into a pan, then get ready for the best part—the topping. To make it, you’ll combine some breadcrumbs and the remaining half cup of Parmesan in a bowl, then add the olive oil and mix it all up. Sprinkle it on top of the mac and cheese in the casserole dish.

All you have to do is pop it into your preheated 375° oven and bake it until it's golden brown on top. Go ahead, snag a bite before it's fully cooled—you'll really be able to taste all your extra effort.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

If you’re looking to make this dish ahead of time, prepare the mac & cheese up until step 4, then cover it in your baking dish and refrigerate it up to 3 days (or freeze it up to 2 months). When ready to serve, add the Parmesan and panko mixture, bake, and serve. If baking from frozen, allow to thaw in the refrigerator overnight before baking.

If you have any leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the fridge for around 3 days.

#6664. Jewelry Designer Keri Ataumbi’s Guide to Santa Fe

Santa Fe is a perennial favorite for avid hikers and art lovers alike—but visit in winter, and you may just have some of its famed galleries and museums to yourself. Crowds thin out, skiers populate the trails, and glowing farolitos take over every public space. (Abiquiú, the onetime home of Georgia O’Keeffe where you can now visit her studio, is a short car trip away.) “Santa Fe has a lot of day hikes, lake trips, and soaks at the local hot springs,” says Keri Ataumbi, a Kiowa artist and fine jewelry designer based in town. You won’t run out of things to do on a winter trip out West; even the non-adventurer will find plenty to delight in.

It’s an excellent shopping destination, too: Santa Fe has a strong Native American artist tradition, and jewelry lovers especially will want to take note. We spoke to Ataumbi for all her best recommendations on where to find the best of it all—plus, a really good cocktail after a day of exploring it all. Just don’t forget the sunscreen; even in winter, the high altitude makes the UV glare intense.

For a one-of-a-kind clothing find: I’m a big fan of owning fewer, quality pieces that last. One of my current favorite tops came from Workshop and Wildlife; it’s an oversized, loose knit, hand-painted cashmere sweater by Avant Toi. Chocolate and Cashmere carries locally knit fine cashmere and locally made beautiful chocolates—I just bought one of their cozy serapes as a birthday present for myself last week. They have a large assortment of colors in the store.

For unique souvenirs: I think the best gifts are consumable, and Kakawa Chocolate House makes both beautiful and unusual chocolates. I love their elixirs, which range from historic pre-Columbian and old European recipes to contemporary creations.

For vintage gems: Double Take is great for treasure hunting, with everything from western boots and statement jewelry to vintage coats and kids’ clothing. Santa Fe Vintage is also fun, but it’s by appointment only.

For a worthwhile investment piece: I wear glasses everyday all day, so they are an essential part of how dress, and I’m an avid collector. Ojo Optique is locally owned and carries handcrafted frames you won’t find everywhere; plus, the owners are wonderful at choosing styles that flatter your face.

For the magpie: There’s so much amazing jewelry in Santa Fe! For Native American jewelry, I love Shiprock Santa Fe and the Case Trading Post. For something not Southwestern, The Golden Eye on Don Gaspar has been making high karat gold jewelry since 1971.

For your next great read: I just picked up a copy of American Bread by Andrew Coe at Garcia Street Books. Then I grabbed a coffee next door at Downtown Subscription and happily lost far too much time reading in their garden under the autumn sun.

For stylish home goods: For something special and unique, I head to the farm store, Los Poblanos Norte.

For the quickest way to impress an out-of-towner: Take a day trip to Truchas to visit Eight Million Gods, where owner Heywood Simoneaux curates a perfectly eclectic store. Back in town, I love Gray Matter. On my last visit, they were unpacking medieval winemaking tools from a French museum; the Cooper’s adzes were my favorite.

For a bakery treat: I love everything at Dolina Bakery and Café, but the gingerbread tiles are my favorite. Owner Annamaria O’Brien is from Slovakia, so the locally sourced menu has Eastern European flavors.

For a fabulous dinner reservation: For a special dinner that’s still relaxed, I go to Izanami. It’s tucked into the mountains and serves small Japanese plates meant for sharing.

For the art-lover: Cara Romero Studio is a photography studio that also hosts group shows, run by my dear friend Cara, an internationally recognized Chemehuevi artist. Her work is deeply thoughtful, with beautifully saturated theatrical compositions.

For an apéro.. or a nightcap: Last month when a friend visited from New York, we had gorgeous cocktails at As Above, So Below, a local distillery that uses local ingredients. Mine was made with fragrant juniper and piñon Sigil gin, butterfly pea flower tea, and a 24k gold garnish.

For your packing list: Do not forget a water bottle and electrolytes—it’s 7,000 feet and very dry, so staying hydrated helps with possible altitude sickness. I love Larroudé sneakers for practicality in Santa Fe, where there are a lot of rocky and uneven surfaces to traverse around town, and my go-to cotton travel trouser is a barrel-leg pair from Nili Lotan. The high desert is extremely dry, so I also recommend the piñon body oil, which is locally made from Dryland Wilds.

#6663. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

Creamy grape salad is a Southern side dish staple. To make it, toss fresh grapes (use both green and red grapes for a colorful dish) in a sweetened mixture of cream cheese and sour cream until they're evenly coated. Then, top with chopped pecans for the perfect crunch to balance out the creamy dressing. In a small bowl, stir pecans and brown sugar. Top salad with pecan mixture. Enjoy!

#6661. Why Men Are Posting Thirst Traps in Red Light Face Masks

Gonzalo Fernández Escribano knew all about the benefits of red-light therapy for his skin. Fewer wrinkles, a brighter complexion, minimizing acne—he’d experienced it all firsthand when he tried out LED masks during his facials. In March 2025, he purchased one for at-home use. Little did he know it would come with an extra benefit as a provocative prop for a sexy photo.

"I use my red-light mask right before bed, so I’m already shirtless,” says Escribano. “Let’s just say the sexy-looking picture is easily convenient to take.”

Escribano is one of many men online who’ve embraced the red-light thirst trap. More and more, image-conscious guys with followings built around some combination of beauty, fitness, wellness, travel, are pairing their red-light routines with the occasional shirtless selfie. The trend is especially prevalent in gay-male internet culture, where faceless torsos shots, sometimes featuring beefy chests and six-pack abs, have been part of the visual language of dating apps and social media for years. A shirtless red-light-mask pic is a variation on the theme: The body and the anonymity are still there—only now there’s a skincare routine attached.

Jayson Stacy, a celebrity groomer, noticed his friend wearing an LED in his Instagram profile picture three years ago. At the same time, Stacy had recently gotten a mask himself and decided to follow suit, posting a photo of his own after Mardi Gras under the guise of some much needed recovery.

“It’s almost like a sexy Halloween costume, but you don’t have to wait until October,” Stacy says. Escribano agrees, saying it makes him look like a superhero. Strong shadows, glowing skin, and a Sith-like red glow mix together in a thirsty trifecta meant to slow someone’s scrolling.

For Stacy, red-light masks strike the perfect balance between wellness and plausible deniability. “You’re supposed to use the mask after you wash your face, so most are fresh out of the shower before using,” he says. “It’s like, ‘Oh, look at my morning routine,’ which gives the perfect excuse to be mostly unclothed. Then you have the mask on, you feel like someone can’t see your face, so it can feel like a layer of protection.” In other words, the skin care routine becomes the reason for the thirst trap, even though it’s only half the motivation.

Red-light therapy is a noninvasive treatment that uses low-level LED light to stimulate cellular activity and boost collagen production. The technology has become especially prominent over the last few years thanks to its ability to reduce inflammation, soften fine lines, and promote skin and muscle recovery and hair growth. (That is, as long as you are willing to invest in high-quality equipment and use it every single day).

Celebrities have been documenting their LED routines for years, from January Jones to Kim Kardashian. But those posts were mostly framed around the masks’ intended purpose: improving your skin. Somewhere along the way, though, a certain breed of extremely online men—trainers, models, artists, content creators, and guys who simply know their angles—found a second purpose for the masks: as an accessory for a hot photo. The masks are turning up in bathroom mirror pics, bedroom shots, and buried several slides deep in otherwise unrelated photo dumps, often without any mention of skin care at all. And judging by the comments—fire emojis, heart eyes, and the occasional “yummy”—their followers seem to be noticing something other than the mask.

The thirst traps are also surfacing on social media at a time when curiosity around red-light therapy is booming. A 2025 study analyzing Google Trends data found that search interest across red-light-therapy-related terms increased 118% after February 2024. And by 2025, Google reported that searches for “red light therapy” had reached an all-time high. As these futuristic devices have rapidly flooded our feeds, maybe it was only a matter of time before they made their way out of the skin care selfie and into something a little thirstier.

In some ways these images are being ushered into well-trodden territory. In 2021, TikTok’s viral Silhouette Challenge had users transform themselves into barely distinguishable, body-forward silhouettes under a red filter, turning the color itself into a visual shorthand for sex appeal. Meanwhile, for gay men, shirtless photos are hardly a novelty, especially on dating apps like Grindr and Sniffies, where headless torsos are practically part of the experience. “The headless torsos definitely all blend together at this point,” says John Arthur Hill, who compares swiping through hookup apps to looking into “a lukewarm batch of Chili’s skillet queso” and trying to figure out what’s cheese, meat, or a bell pepper.

And even when the most impressive six-pack can get lost in an endless doom scroll, red light can add just enough intrigue to get someone to look twice. For Adam Pent, an OnlyFans creator who’s no stranger to posting thirst traps himself, that curiosity is part of the appeal. “It [a red-light-mask thirst trap] is definitely more interesting because I’d be curious about who’s behind the mask,” he says. To Pent, there’s something creative about the whole thing. “I guess it makes the photo a bit more artful too? ‘Art thot’ vibes I guess, unless it looks like sponsored content.” It also makes him want to shop. “I’m less focused on the body and more like, ‘Should I just get one already?’”

The red-light thirst trap also holds a certain mysterious appeal. “I’ve been posting ‘masked’ selfies for quite some time because I think it’s a really hot aesthetic and such a cool fantasy,” Michael Anthony, a celebrity makeup artist, says. For him, it’s not just about looking good in the photos. “The fantasy of anonymity and pleasure, while doing something for yourself that will make you look and feel better—it’s all so sexy.”

Tattoo artist Alvin Archibald sees a similar appeal. “There’s a subtle tension between vulnerability and control that makes it interesting,” he says. “The mask takes away your facial expressions, so the body becomes the focus. It creates this interesting dynamic where you’re both exposed and concealed at the same time. There’s something almost intimate about it, like you’re getting ready for an audience without necessarily admitting it.”

#6660. Where to Stay in Antwerp, Belgium’s Design-Filled City

Antwerp isn’t a loud city. You don’t come here to be awed by ancient ruins or to tour record-breaking skyscrapers. There are no leafy stoops with picturesque brownstones enshrined on TV. Antwerp’s charm unfolds quietly alongside its cobblestoned streets and narrow brick townhouses; I’d argue it’s a place most stumble upon when traveling through Europe, rather than specifically seek out. Those who do make it a point to visit, however, will easily be won over by its unassuming beauty and artistic milieu—after all, there’s a reason why it’s long attracted a certain kind of creative. (Painter Peter Paul Rubens called it home in the 16th century, fashion designers Raf Simons and Pieter Mulier do so in the 21st.)

Winter is an especially lovely time to visit—even when it drizzles (trust me, it will), Antwerp feels delightfully festive: Christmas markets take over the Old Town square, with glowing lights strung up all over the city. The ongoing Antwerp Six exhibit at the MoMu makes a trip this holiday season particularly timely; the group’s first major retrospective closes on January 17, 2027.

The best places to stay in Antwerp offer a chance to adjust to the city’s quiet rhythm—whether that means finding calm in a former convent, or slowing down in one of the many well-appointed Airbnbs that dot the center. Like most major European towns, you can confidently skip the car rental; much, if not most, of Antwerp, can be comfortably discovered on foot and by bike.

An Augustinian convent transformed into a design lover’s dream, the work of famed Belgian architect Vincent Van Duysen makes for a serene refuge after a long journey. Modernist touches and an earthy color palette underscore the property’s monastic qualities, and the rooms are thoughtful but efficiently put together. (The artfully rumpled bed linens are one highlight; the exposed timber beams in the larger suites, another.)

Couples wishing to explore the grounds can unwind with a treatment in the spa—which includes an intimate swimming pond—then dine in the on-site restaurant. (If weather allows, try to book a table in the outdoor terrace.) While the hotel is located in one of Antwerp’s quieter neighborhoods, het Groen Kwartier, you’re still within walking distance from most of the action, including two local favorites: Bar Vert for a low-key lunch, and Funk (an essential personal bookmark) for breakfast pastries.

Photo: Courtesy of Antwerp Botanic Sanctuary

It doesn’t get more central than this. Antwerp’s Botanic Sanctuary, the sole five-star property in town, gets its name from its location: It’s a former monastery nestled besides the city’s Botanical Gardens. Rooms are awash in calming neutrals with multiple large suites available for families—some of which overlook the adjoining 15th-century chapel. Food-motivated travelers are spoilt for choice: Start with drinks at Henry’s Bar, then take your pick of one of three Michelin-starred restaurants for dinner. (Ed note: The property’s marquee wellness facilities are currently temporarily closed due to a recent fire.)

Hotels in European Old Towns aren’t exactly known for their modern charm—and yet, Hotel Julien is brimming with exactly that. Set across two former historic buildings, it precedes the opening of its sister property August, but remains a worthwhile destination for its location alone. Rooms are cozy but pared back, punctuated by touches of red, and you’ll appreciate all the sightseeing there is to do, starting with the rooftop terrace that overlooks the Cathedral of Our Lady—an exalted edifice of Gothic architecture. It’s the ideal cozy home base for a trip spent exploring: “Antwerp is a very historic city, so it’s worth spending a day wandering through its streets, admiring the old architecture, and stepping into the many independent boutiques and antique shops,” adds de Geyter.

Originally a mansion built in 1890, Boulevard Leopold has found new life as a bed and breakfast since 2006. It’s very much no-frills—the aforementioned breakfast, a daily spread that includes croissants and fresh orange juice and is served each morning in the orangerie, is pretty much the only standard “amenity”—but that doesn’t mean it’s sparse. On the contrary, this jewel box of a space is full of charming little touches everywhere you look, the effect of which is a collected feel akin to that of a slightly eccentric aunt’s home.

To wit: crystal chandeliers that play against antler mounts, taxidermy birds that mingle with ornate, gilded candlesticks, a large bamboo fan moonlighting as a headboard that sits above a spartan cot. There are just five bedrooms to book, one of which is a gold-painted suite that takes up the entirety of the first floor. If you’re looking for a quiet, design-forward spot, this B&B is it.

Art is the main motivator at Hotel Pilar, a stylish boutique stay in Antwerp’s hip Het Zuid area, where each of its 21 rooms is designed around unique works. Oil paintings and glossy photographs contrast exposed brick and raw concrete in some; colorful prints juxtapose stainless steel and marbled tiles in others. Lively cafés and bars surround the property, which also happens to overlook the Royal Museum of Fine Arts (KMSKA). For the intrepid gallery hopper, the Museum of Contemporary Art (M HKA) is similarly close by; so is the Ann Demeulemeester flagship if you’re down for a side quest. An art-filled salon adjoins the hotel’s ground-floor restaurant—you’ll want to bookend the day here on one of its velvet couches, no matter where you dined that night.

Set in a 19th-century building in the heart of Antwerp’s fashion district, this light-filled apartment is a more than comfortable base from which to explore the city. It sleeps up to four, with a large dining room and sweet little kitchen that encourages culinary creativity. Original features, like a marble fireplace and antique wood floors, mix seamlessly with modern amenities; you will feel instantly at home.

Stained glass windows, zellige tiling, gilded mirrors… there are more than enough special decorative touches in this home to keep the eye busy. This stay is ideal for a family: It sleeps 10, with five distinctly designed bedrooms (the flamingo pink one, complete with a crystal chandelier and brocade drapes, feels especially grand). It’s well-located, too, with a green park nearby and several main tramlines on your cobblestoned doorstep.

#6659. We Found The 6 Strongest Drinks At Starbucks, Ranked By Caffeine

Each of these bevvies delivers a serious buzz.

I would love nothing more than to be the type of person who jumps out of bed with the sunrise—without the lure of a steaming hot and very caffeinated cup of coffee waiting for me. But I need to smell the freshly brewed espresso before I can muster the strength to get out from under the duvet.

Even as decaf this and half-caf that have become all the rage in our high-cortisol society, you can pry the double cappuccino out of my cold, dead hands! Sometimes you just need a 350-milligram latte to keep you chugging through the day (unless your doctor says otherwise, in which case, ignore me).

In the spirit of staying fueled, I analyzed the Starbucks menu and narrowed it down to the most caffeinated bevvies you can buy in a grande size. However, everything is customizable and may differ slightly in caffeine content—you can always ask for more or fewer espresso shots, or opt for a larger size.

There’s a reason you might feel extra jittery after a morning Cold Brew. It’s packed with caffeine because it uses almost twice as many coffee grounds as regular brewed coffee. It is diluted with water, though, to temper the buzz.

A Caffè Americano—hot or iced—packs a similar punch as a Cold Brew. It’s not all that different, TBH, except instead of brewed coffee, it combines water and espresso to give it a littleeeee more edge.

If you love a sweet latte but want more caffeine, the Iced Brown Sugar Shaken Espresso is your ticket at roughly 255 milligrams for a grande.

If you’re craving a Cold Brew with a kick, go Nitro. It uses a higher coffee-to-water ratio in the cold steeping and dispensing process, and it is served without ice (so, again, less dilution). The result: bold flavor and about 280 milligrams of caffeine.

There’s a reason I’m a drip-coffee loyalist, and it’s not just the flavor. It’s also about the 310 milligrams of caffeine that a grande Pike Place delivers, which earns the medium roast coffee a solid second spot on this list.

Drumroll, please! The most caffeinated beverage on Starbucks’ menu is the Blonde Roast Brewed Coffee at 360 milligrams. Why does it differ from the medium and even the dark roast? It’s pretty simple: Blonde usually tests higher because Starbucks brews it with a little more coffee, and lighter roasts can pack more grounds into the scoop. That means more caffeine makes its way into your cup.

#6658. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6657. APC Just Dropped a Pair of Incredibly Clean Casios

We’re in a great era for affordable fashion-collab watches. Timex is leading the way: its link-ups with Noah, Todd Snyder, and J. Crew are masterclasses in adding personality to classic designs without going OTT. But don’t count Casio out of the race. The Japanese giant has just followed up its 2024 collab with APC. The pair are perfectly matched: Casio watches are known for being beautifully functional and understated—adjectives that fit APC’s spartan aesthetic too.

The first collaboration between the two brands saw them rework the hallowed A1000 digital-display watch. That release stripped back a lot of the original’s markings and added the APC logo on the dial. This time around, it's the AQ-240 getting a makeover. The case is squarer than the rectangular A1000, and while there’s a narrow window for a digital display, the watch maintains the traditional analog format with hands and hour markers. Here, you get the best of both worlds. The watch is sold out on APC's website but still available through Casio, so act fast if you want one. The silver variant is $110, and the gold goes for $135.

What about the APC-ness of it all? That part is the opposite of loud: as with the previous collab, there isn’t much giving away the brand's participation. We’ve got the APC logo on the dial and the buckle, plus the brand’s guitar-and-dagger insignia engraved out of sight on the caseback. Casio already offers the regular A1000 in a bunch of different colorways, but these two new ones are made specifically for the APC collab. The release includes a silver case with a dark-green dial and another in gold on gold. Both of the pieces have a brushed sun-ray effect on the dial. The vibe is refined and stripped back; this is a fashion watch that almost feels anti-fashion.

Maybe the best way to think about it is as the reverse side of the coin to the excellent new G-Shock 2500 Series. Both come from Casio, and both are minimal and functional. But the G-Shocks are big and bulky, with a design that seems to tip its hat to Patek Philippe’s Nautilus. These new ones are slim and nearly dressy. Put the two new releases together, and you’ve got pretty much all bases covered. And if those aforementioned Timex collabs felt a bit too classicist for you, then the Casio-APC partnership takes things in a more modern direction. Far from just being a cash grab, the “fashion watch” is now one of the best routes into affordable, on-point horology.

This story originally appeared on British GQ.

#6656. The 8 Best Hotels in Santa Fe for a Winter Escape

Whatever expectations you might have for Santa Fe, nothing really prepares you for the magnitude of its beauty. The blue sky is enormous—with impossibly fluffy clouds—stretching on and on until it melts into the distance. The surrounding Sangre de Cristo (“blood of Christ”) mountains are especially striking, named by the Spanish who were spellbound by the peaks that turned a vivid red during sunrise and sunset. There’s the traditional adobe architecture the Southwest is famous for, earth-toned and low-slung, and the piñon-juniper woodlands that add to the landscape’s dreamlike quality. It’s a magical place where chiles and pine nuts are on every menu, and the craft scene is so prolific the city was designated a UNESCO Creative City of Crafts and Folk Art. For travelers who have their sights set on New Mexico’s capital city, the best hotels in Santa Fe celebrate its many riches.

The city’s high-elevation desert climate makes visiting throughout the year a distinct experience. In winter, Santa Fe puts on its party hat and transforms into a holiday snow globe with glowing farolitos and city streets perfumed with piñon pine drifting from kiva fireplaces. Whether you choose to position yourself downtown in proximity to galleries and restaurants, or on the outskirts with wild acreage as your backyard, a winter spent in Santa Fe is certain to be a memorable one.

As you plan your upcoming travels, let Vogue’s guide to Santa Fe’s best hotels, below, serve as motivation to spend the cozy season in the Southwest.

Originally settled over 150 years ago by Jean Baptiste Lamy (the first Archbishop of Santa Fe), this property is now home to a luxury retreat surrounded by 317 acres bordering the Santa Fe National Forest. Guest rooms occupy adobe-style structures, with interiors that lean into the southwestern aesthetic—think, kiva fireplaces, wood beam ceilings, and decor sourced from local artists. The resort’s Adventure Basecamp acts as a meeting point for the day’s excursions, which range from horseback riding and guided hikes to a dedicated Ski Santa Fe experience in the winter.

For travelers who prefer a hotel amidst all the action, Vogue’s Senior Fashion and Style Writer Christian Allaire suggests Rosewood Inn of the Anasazi. “If you’re looking to explore around downtown Santa Fe, there are few better locations than here,” he says. “Situated right on the plaza, it's just steps away from all the action—but you may not want to leave, given how cozy the hotel is! The rooms come with wooden beams and fireplaces, and the restaurant serves up classic New Mexican fare with a modern twist.”

Despite its central location, the property feels like its own world once you step through the hand-painted, carved-wood doors. The interiors pay tribute to ancestral textiles and works by local indigenous artists, and chef Cristian Pontiggia (a James Beard Award semifinalist) blends New Mexico ingredients with global influences.

Set on 57 acres in the Sangre de Cristo foothills, Four Seasons Resort Ranch Encantado is a destination for travelers who want to be completely surrounded by nature (yet still situate themselves a convenient 10 minutes from the downtown area). There are 65 casita-style rooms designed with traditional materials like stucco exteriors, wood beams, and kiva fireplaces—plus private outdoor spaces for taking in bird chirps and the afternoon breeze. Thanks to the surrounding wilderness, activities run the gamut, from jeep tours to snowshoeing. Once you’ve worked up an appetite, head to Terra for roasted poblano leek bisque and an Ember & Adobe reposado cocktail.

With its convenient Barrio de Analco location and jewel box interiors, it’s no surprise The Inn of the Five Graces has won several prestigious design and travel awards over the years. “Each room is a feast for the eyes,” Abbas says, “a tapestry of colorful textiles, mosaic tiles, and handcrafted antiques that combine Southwestern decor with East Indian and Tibetan influences.” (If you fall in love with the decor and want to bring home a souvenir, the owners are also behind the furniture store Seret & Sons, which houses their grand collection.) For travelers staying on the property this winter, don’t miss seasonal activities like holiday tea time, fireside cocoa, and a holiday makers market.

This is not your average motel. This adobe roadside motor court was originally built in 1936 and is now home to one of Santa Fe’s most compelling boutique hotels. El Rey Court sits along old Route 66 and offers 86 rooms on five acres of old-growth gardens. No two adobe rooms are identical, and amenities like a heated outdoor swimming pool, a tree-lined lawn, and al fresco fireplace offer plenty of opportunities to soak in the natural surroundings. Be sure to spend at least one of your evenings at Le Reina, their mezcal and tequila bar that serves up a mean margarita.

This legendary hotel on Santa Fe’s iconic plaza sits on land that has played host to an inn since the early 17th century. La Fonda’s current structure dates back to 1922, and is now a member of the Historic Hotels of America association. Original details like hand-carved beams, terracotta tile, and stained glass skylights set a thoroughly romantic tone, while guest rooms keep it cozy with hand-painted headboards and earth tone decor.

For a home-away-from-home kind of getaway, this welcoming bed and breakfast offers eight rooms tucked among lush gardens. El Farolito is close to the city’s best attractions—to name a few: the historic plaza, farmer’s market, and Georgia O’Keefe Museum—yet sits on a tranquil street away from the bustle. The inn features original artwork throughout, as well as handmade furnishings like wood-carved headboards. And be sure to set your alarm for breakfast: It’s served from 7:30 to 9:30 every morning and can be blissfully enjoyed on the patio next to a gurgling fountain.

Unlike local lodging that leans into Southwest design aesthetics, the ryokan-style accommodations at Ten Thousand Waves offer a distinctly Japanese perspective. The spa is surrounded by 20 acres of piñons and junipers, and guest rooms are situated within a historic ranch house. This retreat is best for wellness-focused travelers, as the private hot tub suites and shared soaking environments are just a few steps away from the rooms. (Don’t sleep on the myofascial facial or shiatsu massage, either.) For cuisine, Izanami is an upscale izakaya serving seasonal small plates meant to share.

#6655. 23 Healthy Breakfasts That'll Keep You Full Till Lunch

When it comes to healthy breakfasts, free yourself to eat more than plain yogurt and granola bars. And honestly, those $19 acai bowls from the smoothie shop aren’t that nutritious. A truly healthy breakfast has plenty of carbs for energy (this includes fiber-rich ingredients like whole grains, berries, legumes, and seeds); muscle-and-bone-supporting protein; and plenty of healthy fats for nutrient absorption. Many of these recipes can easily be made ahead and doled out from the freezer, so before you swing by the drive-through for bland egg muffins, consider these more flavorful options. Here are 23 of our favorite healthy breakfasts.

Frozen or fresh berries work great in these accidentally vegan pancakes (thanks, silken tofu!) from Good for You. A good drizzle of maple syrup is all they need for accompaniment, but since I’m not vegan, I enjoy them with a swipe of Greek yogurt.

You maybe haven’t seen an omelet filled with sliced apple and cheddar, but I recommend trying before knocking.

Oatmeal is an ideal choice in the morning for carbs and fiber. I like to slowly stir in egg whites while it’s simmering on the stove for extra protein and top it with ground flaxseed.

A great option for weekend mornings. You could top it with feta or yogurt, dunk whole wheat toast in the sauce, or spoon it over rice, anything goes.

Nothing hits quite like a breakfast burrito, but I can’t buy one every day and still pay rent. DIY to the rescue: I line the tortilla with salsa or hot sauce and sometimes add leftover refried beans if I have them.

The texture of chia seed pudding took me some time to get used to, but now I’m obsessed. Strange how the body adapts! I love that this recipe makes enough for a workweek of breakfasts. Head here for our favorite matcha powders.

If you don’t have time to make the hot honey mixture, these simple breakfast tacos are great with any hot sauces or chile-based condiments that happen to be in the fridge.

This Persian egg dish is similar to a frittata, which means it makes for great meal prep. It takes awhile to wash all the herbs, so make sure you have time, but leftovers will last a few days in the fridge. I like it cold with a swipe of Greek yogurt, but you do you.

Meet the bran muffins you’ll actually crave. Squidgy dates and chopped chocolate make these more like a hearty breakfast cake than the dense pucks you may have eaten in the past.

If it’s not heirloom tomato season, opt for smaller cherry or Campari tomatoes in this recipe—your taste buds will thank you.

To bulk up this green smoothie into a filling meal, add some nut butter and cottage cheese or plain yogurt, plus a scoop of protein powder if you have it.

Leftover cooked quinoa mocking you in the fridge? Stir it in to these blueberry muffins. Win-win.

Speaking of leftover quinoa, if you’re looking for a savory option instead of sweet, throw together this morning salad with a few boiled eggs and smoked trout.

While I personally love mushy porridge, I understand that cakey is a more pleasant texture for many. If that’s the case for you, baked oatmeal is the solution.

Serving brunch to a crowd? Make this breakfast casserole. Just grab a nice loaf of sourdough to slice alongside.

If you haven’t yet tried fried eggs that were based with turmeric oil, now is your moment.

For the savory oatmeal fans out there, try simmering with instant dashi powder and salt-softened vegetables.

A homemade gluten-free loaf that you’ll dream about. Try it with butter and a slice of aged cheese like cheddar or cream cheese and smoked fish.

#6653. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.
