#6632. How to Play GTA 6 All Weekend Without Destroying Your Body

The day has finally arrived. Grand Theft Auto VI is here, and you’ve taken that “sick day” to cause chaos on the streets of Vice City. After more than 10 years of waiting, you’re finally back in one of the franchise’s most classic locations, this time with an open world to explore. It’s not hyperbole to call this the most highly anticipated game in history. With more than 17 million preorders, that’s a lot of people who will be running from the police while trying to avoid (or rack up) six stars.

If you’re one of the many fans who’ve cleared out their schedule to binge the game this weekend, you’ll want to make sure you emerge from your haze with extremities that still function.

“The metaphor we like to share with pro players or casual gamers is the concept of the health bar,” says Dr. Matthew Hwu, owner of physical therapy clinic 1 Health Point in Monrovia, California. “The muscles and tendons of your wrist, hand, thumb, as you move the analog stick, only have so much capacity or ‘max HP’ that they can handle throughout the day.”

Below, we spoke with Dr. Hwu and other veteran gamers about how to keep your “HP” bar full for your whole weekend without developing carpal tunnel.

Playing a game for long hours puts the soft tissues in your hands and arms into overdrive. When you ramp things up, you’ll feel sore and fatigued. The most common version of this is “tendon-based problems of the wrist and hand,” says Dr. Hwu, who has spent more than 11 years working with e-sports players to help them recover from injuries. As GTA 6 will be available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S and X, most people will be using a controller, which puts the thumbs under a lot of stress as people “control the analog stick to flip left, up, right, down; press A, B, X, Y.” The most common gaming injuries are gamer’s thumb and tennis elbow, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

So, don’t forget to take breaks. Dr. Hwu recommends at least a five-minute break for every 90 minutes played, though younger players are more resilient. If you want to push it, the key is taking longer breaks afterwards. “Two hours, 10-minute break, three hours, 15-minute break,” Dr. Hwu says. “If you want to be degenerate, you can be a smart degen.” You can also be strategic about scheduling more downtime after sequences with higher APM (actions per minute), that are more intensive on hand muscles. In essence, go touch grass after a high-stakes bank robbery.

That said, after more than a decade of waiting for what our reviewer described as “the most technically and artistically impressive game world ever made,” your instinct may be to lock in. So it’s wise to plan for breaks ahead of time. Set alarms on your phone or watch. If one goes off in the middle of a mission, commit to taking a break after crashing that helicopter. Make sure you eat and stay hydrated, and move your body, whether that’s a neighborhood walk or just a short twirl around your apartment before your next mission.

“It’s basically just your muscle and tendon tissue recovery, it’ll restore a little bit of HP over time,” Dr. Hwu says. “When you go out and walk outdoors, that can help with your overall circulation, nervous system as well. So you don’t feel like that meme where you come out of the cave and you’re like a ghost.”

Just like in other forms of training, stretching is a key part of your self-care arsenal for long hours of gaming. To loosen up for a long stretch of car-hijacking, do a few stretches before turning on your console, and during cut scenes. Your body will tell you what areas feel tight and could use some attention. But don’t forget those thumb muscles. “Bring your thumb away from the next finger, stretching it down,” Dr. Hwu says. “Every time you’re flicking back, left, or right, you might be using these muscles.”

You’ll also want to stretch your index fingers after long hours of beating ass with a crowbar while riding your motorcycle. “Every time you press your trigger,” Dr. Hwu says, “you’re using the extensors, the top side of your fingers, but also the flexors to push down.” You can also work on relaxing your forearm muscles, by extending your arm out and pushing your palm downward.

Don’t forget your neck and upper back, which can feel stiff from holding onto stress after high speed chases and parachute combat. It’s so easy to load tension onto those upper traps as you shrimp further into your recliner while bird watching, or scoring a pair of black half-rim sunglasses and Eris sneakers (definitely not Nikes) for Jason (no judgment here).

“I will do small things: roll my neck from side to side, stretch my traps by sitting on one hand and pulling my head [in the] opposite direction,” Calliope Ryder, platform director at GYLD, previously a producer on Tales of the Shire, says. “[I] tense my calves in spurts to help with blood flow, or stand up and let my body fold at the hips while swaying side to side with my arms crossed. Again, alerts to remind me to do it are necessary or I'll go hours without noticing.”

Meanwhile, using a heating pad or an ice pack on a sore area (like your lower back) can help with any nagging dull pain you’re feeling. Heat loosens up stiff muscles, while ice can help dull the achy sensation. They won’t build your long-term strength, but they’ll make you feel better in the moment.

If you’re old enough for back pain, then you’re old enough to have to consider video game ergonomics. Wherever you’re gaming, Dr. Hwu’s recommendation is simple: Sit with your legs at a 90-degree angle, feet planted on the ground, back appropriately supported. Then put a pillow on your lap and rest your arms on it. This helps prevent forearm strain and hunching over. You can even haul your expensive Aeron from your office into the living room, rather than rotting on the sofa and ruining your back.

There are also a number of helpful gaming peripherals. Maddy Myers, editor in chief and co-founder of video game publication Mothership, uses a specific gaming pillow from a brand called Mechanism. “The pillow allows you to have the handheld device suspended in the air in a comfortable, adjustable spot so that you don’t tire out your arms from holding it up,” she says. “You can also put a controller on there.”

Using the device helps her get through play stretches of eight hours a day on the weekends, “while taking breaks to eat, do chores, stretch.” It’s been especially invaluable during high-intensity work periods. “I have to play GTA 6 for my job, so I am really going to be relying on these tools to keep my arms and body feeling as close to normal as possible,” she says.

Don’t let a terribly designed controller be the reason you develop carpal tunnel. Julia Lee, section lead for video game guides at Polygon, plays at least two hours of games a day, and will sometimes fit in 10-hour sessions. Her wrists started hurting and “those flat [Nintendo Switch] Joy-Cons were directly to blame,” she says. “I ended up getting a Nintendo Switch Pro Controller (which has a much more ergonomic shape and grip), and that helped alleviate pain a lot.” She also reminds herself not to hold the controller so tight, as it causes pain.

As Dr. Hwu explains, some controllers have staggered sticks, while others have an inline design. It all comes down to individual comfort and muscular endurance. He’s helped pro Call of Duty players modify their analog sticks, and has coached people to avoid death-gripping the controller. “If you use a claw grip position, an awkward grip, or a modded controller, that might lead to more stress for certain muscles in your wrist and hand,” he says.

If your hands are really killing you, there’s also the option of switching to another controller style altogether. “Moving two to four of my most awkward hand-based actions from my hands to my feet allows me to play longer,” John Warren, chief marketing officer and cofounder of Glydr, a foot-based video game controller, says. Warren has minicore disease, which causes muscle weakness. “Anytime you have an opportunity to stop overloading your hands while you play, you give your hands a little reprieve,” he says, “it makes your high-precision hand actions more accurate.”

Lastly, if you have existing injuries, and your medical provider has prescribed a brace, actually follow their guidance for how and when to use it. For my part, I use thumb braces called the Push Metagrips, to help support my floppy thumb joints anytime I plan on playing video games for long stretches.

So you’ve done all this work to binge GTA 6, and you’re feeling solid but a little sore. But you want to play for longer periods, snipe with greater accuracy, and fuck around with less fatigue. Consider going to the gym.

Doing exercises for those small muscles and tendons can help you build up that tolerance, like any other form of weight and endurance training. “When you rest, ice, massage, kinesio tape, you know, passive interventions, bracing, all of these things can restore your HP,” Dr. Hwu says. “It does nothing to change the size of your health bar, which represents the tissue’s capacity or your endurance. The way we do that is you can do specific exercises to build up or create a buffer for how much you’re going to handle.”

For any chronic pain, injuries, or conditions, it’s important to work with a physical therapist. I’m currently working with one for repetitive stress injury recovery, and doing exercises specific to playing video games. I do slow wrist curls with a two-pound weight, rotator cuff exercises with a resistance band, and squeeze an egg-shaped stress ball for thumb and forearm endurance. I also train my shoulders and core.

For those who aren’t managing any injuries, training those finger and arm muscles make it easier to game for longer periods. Consistency is key, and so is having reasonable expectations. Dr. Hwu recommends starting once a day, three to four times a week, “on a day where you’re not doing a lot, and then you’ll learn how your body responds to doing exercises within the context of your specific life, and you can make modifications to scale up the aggressiveness or scale down,” he says. As for seeing progress, “it takes four to six weeks for muscles, eight weeks for tendons.”

And don’t forget the stabilizer muscles in your shoulders, which hold up your upper body and support your arms. “I focus on ‘chest opening’ exercises that strengthen your back,” Ryder says. “I tend towards curving forward so I consciously strengthen the 'opposite' muscles so they pull my shoulders back a bit.” She also does chin tucks, to strengthen her deep neck flexors.

Strength training is also a great way to tackle back pain, another common complaint after gaming for hours. “A few years ago I started having extreme back pain when I sat in my office chair,” Gita Jackson, cofounder of video game publication Aftermath, says. They play one to two hours of games a day, but often play marathon sessions when new games come out. “The pain was excruciating, and sometimes my legs would get so stiff I couldn’t walk. Recovery started with physical therapy, and then a new ergonomic chair,” and now they regularly attend pilates.

“I really had no idea that if I wanted to continue playing noodley strategy games without pain that I would have to be a person who works out multiple times a week,” they say.

Maybe you’ve done a little too much, and your arms start to feel heavy as bricks, with thumbs that ache for hours. Even with the best precautions in place, it can happen to any of us.

“If it gets to a point where cumulatively, over days, symptoms are getting worse, maybe reflect and identify what you could change,” Dr. Hwu says. “If things are consistently sharp, or you start to feel some weakness, where when you go and try to pick up something, you’ll want to drop it. That’s a sign that it may be time to make a change in some of the variables that you can control.”

This is when paying attention to your daily habits is key. Instead of freaking out over hand pain, and deciding you need to quit playing cold turkey, you can instead think about what you did during the day that might have contributed to your discomfort. “How much you’re playing, what intensity you’re playing, are you taking breaks, are you exercising, how are you responding to the pain?” Dr. Hwu says. These are all factors in why you might be having pain, and all things to consider modifying. If it truly is tendon fatigue, then the key is finding the right volume of use, rather than quitting altogether.

There are also some signs to look out for that may require medical intervention. Dr. Hwu pointed me to 1 Health Point’s website, which suggests seeking a doctor’s opinion if your wrist looks swollen or bruised, if you can’t move or bear any weight, if your symptoms worsen or spread with rest, or if you experience constant hand numbness, especially if it comes with weakness.

Gaming for long hours ultimately comes down to using your common sense alongside your precious free will. Pay attention to your habits. Commit to taking breaks and stretching between bank robberies and doomscrolling through Snapmatic (in-game social media). Do some preventative exercises while planning out your next mission—with a soundtrack that includes Bad Bunny and Dua Lipa, as well as some ’80s bangers, you’ve already got the music for it. Your hands and arms will thank you, even if the regular people of Leonida probably won’t.

#6631. A Guide to Ceramics That’s Also a Lot More Than That

How to Make a Pot, a new book by Maggie Boyd, a ceramic artist in New York, is a how-to book that works for clay newbies and veterans, as well as those who are only vaguely interested in clay, given that, at its heart, the book is a meditation on life and art.

It is broken into two parts. Part one explores what a pot is and what it means to make one—reminding you that art is a way to interact with the world—while part two, covering the technical side, gets into how every pot is an experience, and that expertise is the result of many well-intentioned but imprecise turns. It’s not a spoiler to say that Boyd’s book is about how we hold the world and care for it, a future hidden in every piece of fresh wet clay.

How to Make a Pot is very smart and fun and serious, as was its author, who—when Vogue talked to her the other day in her studio, in Bushwick—was wearing a vintage 1930s baseball jersey and making pots.

Maggie Boyd: I was teaching a class for friends in my studio—it was a secret little speakeasy class—because I had a lot of friends who wanted to learn ceramics. One of the people who ended up taking the class, who kind of instigated it, was my friend Caleb, who said, “Listen, you should write a book.” And I said, “You know, I’m not sure, but I think I have a book that I wrote already in my brain.” I’ve been teaching for about 15 years and I’ve been working with clay for over 20 years, so everything that is in there is these collected observations from trying to figure out how to explain a process that is so lengthy and cumbersome and dependent on timing and pressure and a sensitivity to the material. There’ve been so many attempts to try to clarify that process for people.

Part one of the book had me thinking of that great line by M.C. Richards, the Black Mountain College ceramicist and writer, who said: “Poets are not the only poets.” It is a series of drawings with very few words, and I am wondering about what made you want to start a how-to book with drawings as opposed to, say, technical diagrams and step-by-step instructions?

Well, I regularly speak in metaphor. I explain things with drawings, all that stuff, and the way that I teach ceramics is through drawing and basically interpretive dance moves! And I hadn’t seen a book that approached teaching ceramics in this way. So the first part is almost like a prayer or meditation or primer—a spiritual primer before you actually even touch the clay. And the point of that is to resensitize the reader, because I think that especially with—well, I hate to name any of the social media platforms, but I feel as if that one platform has made it so that people are like, “Oh, you can make clay really fast! You can make money at it—it’s a business!” There are all these things that it has sort of taken away from the magic of pushing a material that moves.

Yes, because we are so inundated with the search for the ultimate point of productivity. We’re a grind culture. We’re like: How do we turn the most beautiful, calm, mystical experience of interacting with material into profitable business immediately? And that shifts the way we relate to the material. And I wanted to slow us back down.

Because everything tells us that easier is the best way, which reminds me of a conversation I overheard the other day: two ceramicists were talking about the world being taken over by AI slop. It’s a discussion being had these days by so many people making things: drawings, films, clothing, or even sentences.

I’ve been thinking about this non-stop lately because everyone’s always saying, “Oh, AI just makes everything easy. It streamlines everything and it takes away all this effort.” And to hear this makes me so sad because that is the point for me, the effort. I like doing this. I want to do it. AI would take away that experience with the material. There’s so much magic when you interact with the material or a person, and you can’t do that with AI. That’s not the effort I want removed from my life.

Part of the effort, it seems to me, is learning the hard way that, for example, at around 212 degrees, if there is moisture in a piece it will, no matter how potentially wonderful, explode. Right?

It’s a circle of failing and trying. Clay is a rigorous material to understand and you need a lot of help and a lot of tips and a lot of support and a lot of pre-discovered knowledge. So part two is just me telling you what I’ve learned and what worked for me, knowing that it will be imperfectly described and not everything will apply to you. You take whatever you can from everything you read. And what I’ve learned from doing ceramics for so long is every time I go and I talk with a new artist about a new thing, I learn something from them. Because we’re all approaching this material and it has so many forking paths of possible approaches that I’m always like, “Oh, that’s how you do it.” And it always shifts. So in that way, I don’t feel like I need to know everything because I just know what I know. And hopefully that’s helpful.

Was it difficult to describe, say, how to turn a pot on a wheel? Something that is so seemingly simple but complicated? What was the real triumph for you in, I guess, achieving an explanation?

The triumph is when you have a skill that is so innate and just in your body and then you translate that into words, step by step. It’s such a wild writing exercise. Try it at home! Write how it is to take a fork and bring food to your mouth. It was such an eye-opening experience to understand what how-to manuals do. I had to step outside of myself. Sometimes I would even video myself doing something so I could watch and realize, Oh, that’s the order I do it in!

Do you remember the first ceramic piece that you ever made in your life?

In grade two—that’s what you say in Canada, not “second grade”—we got to work with clay, real clay, for the first time. Not Play-Doh, but clay that was going to go in a kiln. And I made a dragon. And I remember I made a super long neck and these, like, Bart Simpson-looking eyes and pinch spikes all the way around along its tail. And I remember I was like: Maybe I’m kind of good at this? Like, I had this sense really early that I understood working with this material.

This tall dragon that was so beautiful, and then I remember that I glazed the whole thing in a forest green, and I loved that it had green eyeballs that matched its skin! Later on, it got lost, so I actually remade it from memory when I was 23, for my dad. I remember because when I made it before, it said: “Maggie, age 6.” And then the second time I wrote: “Maggie, age 23.”

I’ve read about the “Projects Class” at the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design, where you attended; it involved artists from all over—everyone from Lucy Lippard to Dan Graham to Sonic Youth—collaborating with the school, or even sending up proposals for the students to execute.

I showed up and I completely threw ceramics out the window. Because I was like, okay, well, obviously I’m going to be a performance and sound installation artist who lives in a gallery and then maybe secretly sleeps at school and, you know, does all the stuff that you need to do to get your art school yah-yahs out. I took every possible class and had no intention of graduating. I just wanted to stay forever.

Luckily, I got hired to do the after-school programming at this place, the George Dixon Center, a public housing project in Halifax. So I kind of pulled this skill out of retirement and started teaching. And then people in the neighborhood wanted to take classes, and then I was teaching kids that were about four years old. The teacher before me was saying, “Kids are not allowed to touch the wheel until they’re 11 years old,” or whatever. And then as soon as she left, I said, “All right, kids, get on the wheel!” And it was totally crazy and so amazing. I had something that people wanted to learn that I could share. From that point on I was always teaching ceramics.

How did your art school theoretical studies and your pot-making studio skills connect? Did the two skill sets blend together at some point?

I think for a long time they felt separate, and it’s taken until kind of recently for them to fuse comfortably. I thought of [ceramics] as sort of my trade skill, something I could do. I can throw a pot. I can do cups for restaurants. And I just kept getting hired and hired, and really all I wanted was to have a way to be in a studio. Yes, there was this side of me that just wanted to, you know, do all the experiments and sounds and all this stuff, but I started to think that the art world also wants these two instincts to be at odds. And we buy into that because, you know, commerce is king, and it defines things for us instead of our intuition.

Your pieces seem to be as much functional as they are experiments—wondrous functional experiments—which is to say, I guess you resolved something?

I just stopped believing in the hierarchy that was constructed through commerce and the art world. And I just understood that the most important aspect of being an artist is following the impulse to make, because it’s a question that you solve with any answer, and it doesn’t have to have a truth. So you just get to follow this incredible line of thought and that’s the whole point. That could become a pot or painting or drawing or a dance or a nap or whatever—they’re all just the same person asking the same questions and trying to answer them in different ways.

By the way, what happened when the four-year-olds got on the wheel?

OK, the difference between adults and children is that children, if you get them at the right point, have absolutely no fear about making a mistake. They are so fearless and they have so little self-criticality. They’re just pure curiosity and cause and effect. And so, yeah, kids on the wheel is sometimes, “How fast can this thing go?” and “How far can I spray this clay?” Like, pretty good questions, though hard questions to clean up. But they’re just so involved in making, whereas when you teach adults, you have to try to sort of break them back down. Sister Corita Kent, she says: “Don’t try to create and analyze at the same time.” So that’s what children don’t need help with, and it’s exactly what an adult often needs help with. And then, well, if you learn to decipher a pot, a pot will show you who you are.

In terms of part two of How to Make a Pot, what are you reading to continue your never-ending ceramic education?

The Ceramic Spectrum by Robin Hopper, second edition. It is the definitive reference book on glaze.

And for the lay person, such as myself: What, exactly, is a glaze?

So a glaze is a glass-like coating that goes on top of a clay body, that fuses to the surface. It is made up of stabilizer, glass, and flux to make it melt, and its combinations of those three ingredients [dictate] how it holds color, or its opacity or clarity or transparency and all that.

And what are Hopper’s insights into glaze?

He is talking about how experience is so much more important than calculation in glaze-making. It’s just a really great overview of how to make colors and glazes and how to experiment. He values knowledge that is experiential, and it’s so cool because I feel as if glaze-making, in particular, is this gatekept thing—you have to understand the chemistry and how to do the chemical equations. And he just makes the point, which I feel like people need to remind themselves of with almost all things that they make, bread or anything, that this is something that has been part of humanity since long before we had computer programs that broke down the chemical analysis of something.

What have you read recently, or what have you been listening to while you work in the studio at this moment?

A lecture by Anne Carson on Homer’s Odyssey and Le Mépris, the film by Jean-Luc Godard. I used to say my two favorite movies were The Lion King and Le Mépris.

Ah, a film about an artist making a film, and having to deal with the studio’s purely commercial demands, which is what Godard himself was dealing with in dealing with an American producer; the insistence, first off, that Brigitte Bardot be nude!

Yes, and Carson is talking about how to be an artist. Or, really, about the seller versus selling. But until I heard her lecture, I didn’t understand that the Americans asked that he have nudity in the film, and that Godard said, “Oh, so what I’m going to do is I’m going to double down on this thing that you’re asking me to do and actually, like, rub it in your face.” Carson says Godard makes art out of selling out. She says he makes a spectacle of compromise. And she says that Brigitte Bardot just wins. I love that. The film’s so good. It’s how to be an artist, or when do you realize, Oh, they’re just going to want you to make the same thing.

This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6630. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#6629. 11 Non-Traditional Thanksgiving Turkey Recipes That Everyone Will Love (Even The Haters)

These 11 non-traditional Thanksgiving turkey recipes bring all the benefits of a juicy, well-seasoned turkey, with more flavor and flair. This meatloaf is moist and LOADED with flavor, thanks to Worcestershire sauce, fresh herbs, and a simple two-ingredient glaze on top. Whether you’re looking for a lighter alternative or just want to mix things up, this recipe should have a place on your Thanksgiving table.

This herby, savory-sweet dish is basically Thanksgiving in meatball form. With a sweet and tangy glaze made with cranberry sauce and thyme- and sage-speckled turkey meatballs, all you need is a scoop of fluffy mashed potatoes for cozy, autumnal bliss.

Alright, it may not actually be able to take the place of turkey on your table, but this Rice Krispies turkey is too cute not to include. It’s the perfect way to wrap up dinner and make all your guests smile.

#6628. The Best Sparkling Water Maker, Based on Years of Testing (2026)

Dedicating some counter space to a soda maker comes with several benefits. For one thing, these appliances are a great way to cut down on single-use plastic and other waste by eliminating the recycling bags full of bottles, cans, and cardboard boxes you inevitably accumulate with a regular La Croix habit. But they will also save you some money in the long run, as carbonating your own water costs less than buying premade fizz from the store. One standard-size CO2 canister, which should cost roughly $15, can carbonate around 60 liters of water. Considering the $3 cost of a 2-L bottle of Canada Dry, that comes out to around three times as much soda water per dollar.

After years of testing soda makers, I’ve found models that make it quick and easy to make zingy, fizzy drinks (including juice, wine, and cocktails) with the push of a button. Find our top picks below and scroll further down to see what I thought of the machines that didn’t earn a top spot.

New in this update: For this update, I tested two sparkling water makers by Drinkmate: the previously discontinued (and now recontinued) Drinkmate Spritzer and the Drinkmate Lux, which in between testing and publishing was subsequently discontinued and replaced with the new Sparkleup, welp!

Drinkmate Omnifizz Sparkling Water and Soda Maker

Amazon (With 60-L CO2 Tank and Extra Bottle)

Height: 16.14"Machine material(s): PlasticBottle material: PlasticComes with starter CO2 tank: Yes (size varies by retailer)Requires proprietary CO2 tank: NoWarranty: 2 years

Over years of testing, nothing has surpassed the Drinkmate Omnifizz’s mix of versatility and affordability. It is, full stop, the most affordable sparkling water maker that can also do other “fun” carbonating, like wine, cocktails, tea, and (pulp-free) fruit juice.

What I love: The Omnifizz has a well-designed detachable siphon with fast and slow pressure release tabs. It carbonates fast, delivering maximum sharp fizz in around two seconds. This gives you more control when carbonating anything with a syrup or other sugars (wine or cocktails, for example), which fizz up a lot more than plain water. The siphon design also offers a much more secure connection than the machines that require you to pop and/or twist the bottle into the base, which diminishes the likelihood of an accidental soda explosion to the face (which happens to the best of us!)

What I’d leave: In addition to being kind of meh in the looks department (especially in a world where so many brands have placed a focus on the aesthetics of their soda makers), this carbonator is made of all plastic parts, so it doesn’t feel as durable as some others I’ve tested. It also screams like a banshee when its done. Depending on the retailer you order from, it may or may not ship with a CO2 cylinder, so be sure to read the product descriptions carefully.

Height: 16.9"Machine material(s): Stainless steelBottle material: PlasticComes with starter CO2 tank: Only if you buy the bundleRequires proprietary CO2 tank: NoWarranty: 2 years

Breville has cornered the market on high-end small kitchen appliances with its top-performing countertop oven, induction burner, toaster, and immersion blender. In 2024, the brand added a sparkling water maker to that list.

What I love: The Breville Infizz Fusion is a sleek, versatile carbonator, and like the Drinkmate Ominifizz, it will carbonate more than just water. The default setting on the carbonator cap is a slow pressure release that allows carbonation of fruit juice, wine, cocktails, and even creamy drinks if you’re feeling weird. You can manually release the pressure faster if you just need a bottle of fizzy water in a hurry. Unlike the soda makers I liked in the $100 to $150 range, which usually have all plastic parts, parts of the InFizz Fusion are made of durable, high-quality stainless steel, which is available in a variety of finishes, though options vary by retailer. It also comes with a handful of accessories (including a juice filter and silicone bottle brush) to enhance the experience of using and cleaning the machine and bottle.

What I’d leave: Compared to the Drinkmate, this machine is slightly more fussy to operate. Not by much, but I prefer the Drinkmate’s quick click to Breville’s twist-and-lock design. Countertop soda makers are simple gadgets, and this is one of the priciest ones you can buy. If it’s worth it to you to pay for quality materials, aesthetics, and the ability to wow your dinner guests by transforming a bottle of bad rosé into something bubbly and palatable, you’ll likely be very happy with this (FWIW the Drinkmate can also sparkle bad rosé, it just wont look as nice doing it). But do keep in mind that the base model, which is $249 at the time of publishing, doesn’t ship with a CO2 tank, so you’ll either need to buy one or spend $30 more on one that comes with the tank.

Drinkmate Spritzer Portable Sparkling Water

Height: 7"Machine material(s): PlasticBottle material: PlasticComes with starter CO2 tank: Only if you buy the bundleRequires proprietary CO2 tank: NoWarranty: 2 years

What I love: When I first tested the Spritzer several years ago, it was my top pick. But then Drinkmate discontinued it, which was sad, but now, it’s back. At this point I can’t give it the absolute top spot (I’ll get into that down below), but in a more niche position of portable carbonator, I still recommend it.

The Spritzer has all the versatility of Drinkmate’s countertop model in a smaller, portable format. Seeing as the earliest carbonators were portable, it’s almost a return to form. Almost, because the Spritzer looks more like one of those guns that shoots money and not like something you’d see in the hands of an old-timey soda jerk. But much like a gun that shoots money, the Spritzer is very fun to use. In terms of user experience, I prefer the Spritzer’s trigger over the standard, button-on-top-of-the-machine design. It just feels like I have more control over the thing when I use it.

Beyond that, the Spritzer takes up less space and is easy to stow away, and it is also cheaper than the countertop version.

What I’d leave: The Spritzer is designed to use smaller 10-L gas canisters rather than the standard 60-L size. Unless you source them directly from Drinkmate, the 10-L canisters are difficult to find, so you end up being reliant on its exchange program. The Spritzer will still work with a full size canister, but I wouldn’t recommend doing that because it doesn’t fit well in the carbonator and gets a bit unwieldy. Drinkmate also originally had a docking station for it the Spritzer, but unfortunately the brand got rid of it. Ultimately, the reason I don’t give this the top spot is that its design is such a departure from what most people expect in a soda maker it has a much narrower appeal.

With every update I look at the most popular and highly rated countertop sparkling water makers, taking into consideration availability, price, and customer ratings. Then, I judge them on the following:

I first assess how easy it is to use and assemble each machine. Looks matter too, but they aren’t everything. And if a machine can carbonate more than just water (what's up Drinkmate and Breville), that’s a huge plus as well.

I used each machine several times to get a general sense of how long the machine takes to carbonate and the fizz level of each batch. For the first few rounds I follow the manufacturer’s instructions. After that I try pushing the machine to its maximum capability (usually until I hear the hissing of excess gas escaping). If the machine can carbonate more than just water, I’ll do a few rounds with juice and wine.

This simple, stylish carbonator from Finnish brand Mysoda is made from renewable wood composite. It’s beautiful, sturdy, and, when it comes to the level of carbonation, performs as well as any SodaStream. And if you want an aesthetically pleasing, sustainably made, budget-friendly soda maker, you’ll be very happy with this purchase. But there’s a catch to that: Most soda makers ship with a starter CO2 tank, and this one doesn’t. New tanks, not tank trade-ins, cost $30 to $40. So when you factor that into the cost, the initial investment is more than the cost of our top pick, which did perform a little better anyway. If you want to stay under $100 all in, check out the Philips Sparkling Water Maker below.

This Mysoda distinguishes itself from the others with a glass carafe. Anytime I encounter a soda maker that carbonates in glass, I'm suspicious, because I haven’t seen them work well in the past. This might be because soda makers that carbonate in glass tend to be designed with additional safeguards to minimize the possibility of the bottle exploding, and those safeguards are usually fussy. Often they take the form of some sort of cover that goes over the entire bottle during the carbonation process. In the case of the Glassy, the bottle is covered by a curved sliding door that you shut by hand, reminiscent of a changing room curtain or a shower stall.

To use the machine, you place the bottle inside and twist it onto the gas nozzle to lock it in place. Then you shut the door and press the top of the machine toward the front to inject the gas (the top is mostly one large button). After a couple of pumps, you’ll hear a hissing sound, which signals that it’s ready. You then press the top toward the back of the machine, which causes the door to fly open, presenting your carbonated water like a magician’s assistant doing a quick change magic trick. It’s all very dramatic, which is kind of fun.

As far as soda makers that carbonate in glass, this is the best I’ve tried. That said, I'm not sure how important it is to be able to carbonate in glass, especially with the risk (however small) that it will explode into shards with you close by. You can always just carbonate in a plastic bottle and pour it into a glass vessel for serving.

Check out our full review of the Glassy here.

The Philips Sparkling Water Maker is a handsome machine with a comparatively accessible price tag, and it’s easy to set up and operate with one button. More importantly, during testing, it made pleasantly sharp carbonated water. Like the Mysoda Woody above, it doesn’t ship with CO2, so you’ll still need to shell out for a standard screw-in 60-L CO2 tank. However, at the current retail price, even with the addition of a tank, it still comes in at just under $100.

The Aerflo is even easier to tae on the go than the Drinkmate Spritzer. There is a carbonator mechanism inside the lid, which you activate by pressing a button on the top. Instead of full-size CO2 canisters used for most sparkling water makers, it utilizes smaller capsules typically used for airsoft or BB guns. Because of the capsules small size, you will need to swap them much more frequently; one capsule has enough CO2 for about one day’s worth of sparkling water. It’s cool and convenient if you really prefer carbonated water over still. But this is a product for a smaller subset of people than a countertop soda maker. If it appeals to you though, go for it.

Check out my full review of the Aerflo here.

This is the model that came after the now-discontinued Aarke Carbonator II, and the main upgrades are materials. The Aarke Carbonator III has more stainless steel and fewer plastic parts than the II. Both models are highly aesthetic machines that are easy enough to use and make perfectly fine sparkling water. If you like the look of it, you’ll probably be very happy with it, but the Breville is in the same general price range and is more versatile. Plus, there are lower-priced machines that perform just as well.

Awa appears to be selling itself entirely based on aesthetics. Once you move beyond the body design though, this is a standard sparkling water maker with a single button for injecting CO2. It lacks a tilting nozzle or a slide-in lock, which makes it more annoying to use than the winning models. The build is also almost entirely plastic, save for a few metal details, which doesn’t really justify the premium price point. If you like how it looks, it will get the job done, but it’s not innovating on the form.

A frequent complaint people have about sparkling water makers is their reliance on plastic bottles, as many consumers are looking to avoid plastic entirely. The Fizzit is one of the few soda makers that uses metal bottles instead. Apart from that, its design and performance are similar to the other soda makers sharing the same standard design on the market. Were this the only machine on the market to carbonate directly into stainless steel, maybe that would be something, but Sodastream also offers stainless-steel carbonator bottles, and I imagine more brands will follow suit. Also sorry to Spärklï, but the branding on this machine is a bit of an eyesore. If you’re looking for a machine that comes with metal bottles and aren’t a fan of Sodastream though, this might be for you.

The Fritaire carbonator flipped the conventional soda maker design on its head. It’s the only soda maker I’ve tested so far that carbonates from the bottom up, with a fold-up gas nozzle that makes for a slightly more compact machine. The bottle is also different, with mechanical components built in at the bottom, and a wide curved carafe-style lip. Unfortunately I could not get this to produce a satisfyingly sharp bottle of seltzer, no matter how much gas I pumped into the bottle. Where other machines make a clear sound when the pressure has been maxed out, the Fritaire’s was not obvious. The instructions recommend pressing the button for three seconds until you “hear the sound of pressure building.” Each time I tried, the water came out under-carbonated. On top of that, the lid for the bottle dribbled water even when tightly screwed on. I really tried to give this machine the benefit of the doubt, testing and retesting to try and get it not to leak on me and to get a proper fizz, but each time I encountered the same problems no matter what I did.

Smeg is known for its retro-futurist luxury kitchen products that really sell for their looks. This machine worked fine. You twist the metal dial clockwise to carbonate, a clever hidden feature that sets it apart from other carbonators, but it lacks the ability to tilt the nozzle, which makes screwing on the bottle more tedious. For a soda maker made almost entirely out of plastic, the price point is well beyond what it’s worth, but if you’re a Smeg collector, this is another piece to add to your collection.

One of the few new electric sparkling water systems, the Carbon8 is quite different from other machines on the market. Instead of directly carbonating into the bottle, the Carbon8 has a refillable reservoir (much like a drip coffee maker) that instead, dispenses carbonated water straight into your glass. It has added flourishes, like a sanitizing UV light and a filter that remineralizes water while removing chlorine.

The brand implies superior eco-friendliness in their website copy because they don’t carbonate directly into a reusable PET plastic bottle; however, the reservoir and other parts of the machine are made of plastic, so I’m not sure they have much plastic-free ground to stand on. You could argue that since the plastic bottles of typical soda makers have to be replaced every couple of years, this system produces less plastic waste, but it’s a marginal difference in my opinion.

As a premium machine this Carbon8 worked fine, but had one shortcoming: There seems to be no way to control the carbonation level of the machine, and when I tasted the finished product, I found the level of carbonation to be far less than what you’d expect from store-bought seltzer, or what you can produce with the winning machines. If the Carbon8 gave you control over how fizzy you wanted your water, it would make this a much better machine.

Ninja is among the most prolific small appliance manufacturers with coffee makers, countertop ovens, blenders, ice cream makers, juicers, toasters, air fryers—the list goes on and on and on. So it should come as no surprise that the brand is now in the soda maker business too. Like many of Ninja’s other offerings, the Ninja Thirsti is a bit gimmicky while still being kind of cool. Out of the box, this electric soda maker (yes, you have to plug it in) reminded us of a Nespresso machine. The water tank sits off to the side and the carbonation happens inside the machine before coming out of a little spout. There’s an opening on the front to add up to two proprietary flavoring cartridges, which you can put in your bubbly water individually or combine them both. Currently there are 30 flavors available and the machine shipped with four of them. The control panel on the front of the machine allows you to choose between still water or three levels of carbonation, and four drink sizes (6, 12, 18, or 24 oz.). After testing, I have mixed feelings about this machine. Overall, it seems like a bit much for something to have at home. It could maybe be a great addition to a teachers’ lounge or a small office. But keep in mind that the water tank does require chilled, cold water so you’d also need a fridge or ice nearby whenever you want to use it.

If you’ve ever dreamed of having a club soda tap in your kitchen, this is probably as close as you’re going to get without cutting into your countertops. Like the Ninja above, the Glacier Fresh Sparkin Cold Soda Maker carbonates water in the machine, not in a bottle. Unlike the Ninja, the machine chills the water for you (though the manual still recommends filling the reservoir on the back of the machine with cold water). Once it’s filled, getting your bubbly water from the “tap” is a three-step process. First, you push a button to send water from the reservoir to the bubbling (and presumably chilling) chamber, then you push down on a lever to carbonate it. Once it’s sufficiently bubbly, you press another little lever on the front to dispense the water into a glass. It’s less complicated than it sounds, but with an 88-square-inch footprint, most people will be better off with a bottle-style carbonator. I will also note that when moved from the counter to a nearby table with the CO2 canister in place and some water still in the chamber (ill-advised, perhaps), it began to make a weird squealing noise.

The SodaStream Art is marketed as the company’s premium carbonator, because of its retro-inspired body. Though it produces the exact same carbonated water as other SodaStream models, it operates a little differently: Instead of pushing a button to carbonate, you pull the lever and you can pull it up to six times for the bubbliest water. But it’s made of lightweight plastic that feels cheap. If you want something that looks good on the countertop, there are prettier options that are also sturdier.

Aarke carbonators are really easy on the eyes, and this “pro” version doesn’t skimp on materials. Instead of the typical plastic bottles, this one uses glass, and the top of the machine (which is available in a matte black, matte sand, or shiny stainless-steel finish) covers the top of the bottle in case you were to over-carbonate and cause the glass to explode. Unfortunately, it’s not very user-friendly. I had issues getting everything to lock into place and ended up with an explosion—though, luckily, it was only water and not glass. I eventually got it to work, but for the price, it should be easier to operate.

I loved the sleek design of this soda maker in pictures, but in person, the materials felt cheap and flimsy. Also, because it’s so sleek and slim, the water bottles are really tall and didn’t fit into any shelves in a standard sized fridge.

Instead of using a CO2 tank to produce carbon dioxide, this machine uses citric acid and baking soda. The mechanism is just way more high maintenance compared to the machines that utilize a gas canister, and I struggle to see why this method is in any way better than the industry standard.

Currently, the Terra is SodaStream’s most basic offering, and functionally, it’s a lot like the original SodaStream, the Fizzi. However, instead of a screw-in CO2 cartridge, this machine uses the brand’s Quick Connect cartridges, which click in. Because the Quick Connect feature is proprietary, using this machine means being married to Soda Stream’s cylinder exchange program. With products like the Mysoda Woody or the Philips Sparkling Water Maker, you can and should get something with a universal connection.

This style of carbonator is a relic of the 19th century, and while it has an abundance of charm, it’s more tedious, fussy, and impractical than its modern counterparts. It relies on small, single-use CO2 cartridges—which negates the whole eco-friendly argument for carbonating at home rather buying seltzer from the store— and you have to use two cartridges per liter if you like your seltzer extra sharp. Frankly, the only people I’d recommend this to would be that husband and wife on TLC who pretend they’re living in the 1950s.

There is nothing inherently wrong with the E-Duo. Of the carbonators that use glass bottles, it is the easiest to use. It does require a few additional steps to lock the bottle safely into place (just in case that glass bottle explodes!), but I didn’t find the safety mechanisms to be overly fussy. However, as with the Ninja, this soda maker requires electricity. With so many excellent soda makers that function effectively without electricity, I don’t really see the need to use one that does.

#6626. 2026 Earth Partner Prize: The Winners

Earth Partner, Art Partner's sustainability division, in collaboration with the Global Environment Facility (GEF) and Re:wild, has announced the winners of the 2026 Earth Partner Prize, the annual competition inviting artists aged 14–30 to explore different aspects of the ecological crisis through art.

The Grand Prize ($10,000) was awarded to 16-year-old Samuel Bird from the UK for THE GAS WORKS, a 2.1-metre-long linocut print exploring the climate impact of war and the lack of transparency surrounding military emissions. Two Runner-Up prizes ($5,000 each), five Third-Place awards ($2,000 each) and 20 Honourable Mentions were also awarded.

The 28 winning works are now on view in a virtual exhibition powered by Kunstmatrix. Spanning photography, film, poetry, performance, animation and textiles, the projects address issues ranging from retreating glaciers and disappearing pollinators to the environmental consequences of war and the loss of Indigenous knowledge.

All 28 works will also be showcased at the Climate Funds Pavilion during COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, through the Prize's partnership with the GEF.

1st Place ($10k)Samuel Bird (UK), THE GAS WORKS

A 2.1-metre-long linocut print exploring the climate impact of war and the lack of transparency surrounding military emissions. At just 16 years old, Samuel draws on his experience of dyslexia to inform his distinctive approach to working in reverse when designing and cutting linocut prints.

2nd Place ($5k)Radoslav Sviretsov (Bulgaria-Iceland), VEINS OF A CHANGING LAND

As Iceland's glaciers continue to retreat, increasing volumes of meltwater are reshaping the country's river systems. Through his work, Radoslav reflects on the gradual transformation of landscapes and the danger of becoming accustomed to environmental loss.

2nd Place ($5k)Maewenn Bourcelot (France), ETERNAL EPHEMERAL

Through microscopy, colour and shifts in scale, Maewenn draws audiences into the world of pollinators, creating a photographic poem about their disappearance and the gradual, often unnoticed nature of ecological change.

3rd Place ($2k)Aakash Gulzar (India), THE LAST PATTU

3rd Place ($2k)Ishita Sharma (UK) — A WILD HOPE OF UNBOUNDED SEEING

3rd Place ($2k)Cristian Pǎsat and Oxana Capatina (Moldova), GUNOI SUB COVOR: SWEEPING UNDER THE RUG

3rd Place ($2k)Reza Javanshir (Iran), SALT WOUND

3rd Place ($2k)Kaanchi Chopra (India), THE EARTH LAUGHS IN FLOWERS

The artists were selected by an international jury, including Derrick O. Boateng (acclaimed artist and founder of the “Hueism” movement), Dr Robin Moore (photographer and Chief Communications Officer at Re:wild), Dr Musonda Mumba (Secretary General of the Convention on Wetlands), Giovanni Testino (Founder of Art Partner), Marina Testino (sustainability advocate), Hans Ulrich Obrist (Artistic Director of the Serpentine Galleries), Ferdinando Verderi (Creative Director), Marcela Villafaña (Indigenous Arhuaco filmmaker), and Shaway Yeh (pioneer of sustainable fashion in China).

The jury also awarded 20 Honourable Mentions and the Earth Partner Impact Award ($1.5K), recognising the project that best demonstrates the community impact of artistic initiatives led by young people, to ECO-ART BHUTA KALA: THE THIRD SPACE OF WATER GOVERNANCE (Bali), an interactive sculptural installation and community mobilisation project raising awareness of the hydrological challenges faced by local communities.

#6625. Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

In my opinion, corn casserole is the most underrated Thanksgiving side. Let this classic side be the star of your Thanksgiving dinner if you’re ever in the mood for endless praise and compliments.

What People Are Saying:“Very delicious, made it exactly like written, came out perfectly.” - mgnpanossia4246

After greasing your baking dish (very well) with softened butter and preheating the oven, break out that box of Jiffy mix. Whisk the mix with granulated sugar in a bowl until very few lumps remain.

Then mix—in a medium bowl or large measuring cup—your eggs, milk, cream, and melted butter until combined. Add that bowl into your Jiffy mix bowl, and stir until just combined. You don’t have to overmix here. Stir in your (thawed!) corn, creamed corn, salt, paprika, and pepper.

Pour your mixture into your prepared baking dish, using a spatula to smooth out the top. Bake until the casserole has fully set and the top is golden brown. This should take anywhere from 40 to 50 minutes.

Once done, let it cool slightly before serving, and top with fresh chives.

The full ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Since only 10 minutes of prep go into this corn casserole, you’ll have plenty of time to pull together the rest of dinner as it bakes in the oven. Try this with simple air-fryer chicken thighs or a hearty harvest chicken skillet for a comforting weeknight dinner, or add it to your holiday sides of mashed potato casserole, sweet potato casserole, and butternut squash mac & cheese alongside your roast turkey.

If you want to make your holiday easier, then this corn casserole is a perfect make-ahead Thanksgiving recipe. Simply prepare the casserole, then cover it tightly and store it in the fridge for up to 48 hours. Remove and bake once you're ready to serve, keeping in mind that it may take slightly longer to bake coming straight from the fridge.

If you somehow manage to have any leftovers, tightly cover your casserole dish or store it in an airtight container in the fridge for 4-5 days.

#6621. On the Front Lines of the Advent Calendar Wars

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the mysterious hackers hitting refrigeration systems.

I’m starting today’s Open Tab with my favorite thing in the world: a morsel of exclusive news. In chatting with BA alum Alison Roman about First Bloom, her soon-to-open NYC storefront (more on that from me very soon), she told me she’s releasing a new podcast that will be officially announced early next week.

I’m mostly sworn to secrecy until Roman drops the trailer, but I can tell you there will be cooking, there will be guests, and there will be banter. But, she said, this project will be distinctly different from her earlier work. “I’m not going back to Home Movies. I’m just not,” she told me over the phone earlier this week.

Also in today’s Open Tab: How much more ridiculous can advent calendars get? Was this NYC gay bar actually designed by AI? And how is Andy Baraghani thinking about his first restaurant?

Gone are the days when advent calendars were essentially manufactured cardboard inside of which you could find some of the most unfortunate tasting chocolate ever produced. These days we’ve moved beyond chocolate. Some advent calendars open to reveal tinned fish, others jewelry, and still others skin-care products. Google Trends data shows search interest for advent calendars has grown steadily for the past five years, and as writer Emily Bloch reported for Bon Appétit, the global advent calendar market is expected to grow to $2.47 billion by 2033.

Part of the appeal, as Bloch mentions, is the little-treat-culture of it all. It’s nice to open up a little surprise each day. But another element, surely, is the content that’s made around advent calendars. There are the unboxings—tailor-made for the short-form vertical video format which rewards reveals—and there are the scandals. Who could forget (everyone except me, realistically) the backlash against Chanel’s $825 advent calendar in 2021 when customers declared the included products decidedly lackluster? This year Skims faces a similar backlash for its $148 advent calendar for which it is now offering refunds.

But drama and outrage gets attention, which in turn fuels more content. And as the Kardashian clan knows better than most, no matter what the public is saying, at the end of the day they’re still talking about you. Thus, the advent calendar cycle continues for another year, growing ever greater. Will we ever summit the peak of the advent calendar craze? So far, the data say no.

If you’ve read—or even skimmed—this column in the past, you’ve likely gleaned that I often point out the many fumblings of AI—one could argue I make a sport of it. That’s why, when I saw grumblings online that a new gay bar in New York City’s Hell’s Kitchen looked like it had been designed by Chat-GPT, I felt a morbid curiosity begin to bubble. The bar, commenters said, was so deeply on-the-nose gay-bar-coded, it simply couldn’t have been made by a human brain. It was named Pride Bar x Lounge (a bit first thought, right?), and its decor is essentially just rainbow flags. It kind of looks like how they’d design a gay bar in a Netflix show, which is to say: almost impressively bland.

In a report from The New York Times, the two co-owners say that they did not in fact use any AI in designing the bar, which has cost about $5 million so far to come to fruition. On the other hand, the posters released to promote the bar, which had also received some heat, were in fact made using AI.

The saga is an interesting data point in the public’s perception of what is an appropriate way to use this tech: making a grocery list? Sure. Using it to help you figure out what exactly you like about your own child? Absolutely not. Asking AI to help you plan a trip? I guess. Using it to design a gay bar? Hard no.

#6620. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#6619. I Chewed 7 Popular Gum Brands Until They Lost Their Flavor—Here's Which Lasted The Longest

Chewing gum can be incredibly frustrating. You unwrap a fresh piece expecting a burst of minty flavor that'll last a while, only to find yourself chewing flavorless rubber five minutes later. And most of the time, it doesn't even make it that long.

So I decided to put seven popular gum brands to the ultimate test. I would chew each piece until the flavor completely disappeared, timing exactly how long it took before I was left with nothing but a rubbery wad of disappointment.

I judged each gum on the intensity of its spearmint flavor, how pleasant it was to chew, and, most importantly, how long that minty taste actually lasted. And after spending a frankly ridiculous amount of time chewing gum, I have some thoughts (and jaw pain). Here's how all seven brands ranked, from shortest-lasting to longest-lasting.

I quickly knew Pür wasn't going to be a strong contender. Of all seven brands, this had the least flavor right from the beginning. While the other gums delivered at least some noticeable burst of spearmint, Pür barely gave me enough to enjoy before the taste started disappearing.

But the bigger issue was the texture. Almost immediately, the gum became tough and waxy, making it unpleasant to chew even before the flavor was completely gone. Instead of that soft, satisfying consistency I want from gum, it felt like I was working way too hard for very little reward.

By the time I hit one minute and 36 seconds, there was absolutely no reason to keep chewing.

Considering the packaging literally advertises long-lasting flavor, I had pretty high expectations going into this one. Unfortunately, the results were anything but impressive.

The spearmint flavor disappeared after just two minutes and one second, making Extra the second shortest-lasting gum in the entire test. When a brand makes longevity such a prominent selling point, I expect to get more than two minutes of enjoyment out of a piece.

I'm not saying I need my gum to taste fresh all afternoon, but two minutes feels like a pretty low bar. I don't like liars, Extra. And you’re not extra, you’re underwhelming.

Trident managed to outlast Extra and Pür, but not by a particularly impressive margin. The biggest thing I noticed was the texture. This gum leaned more toward the waxy side, which isn't exactly my favorite quality in something I'm supposed to be chewing for an extended period.

The spearmint flavor lasted two minutes and 30 seconds before fading away, putting it firmly in the bottom half of the ranking. While it held on slightly longer than Extra, the difference wasn't enough to make Trident feel particularly long-lasting.

And considering how much better the top four performed, this one simply couldn't compete.

Orbit immediately impressed me with a very strong burst of mint flavor. Compared with the previous three brands, the initial taste was much more noticeable, making the experience more enjoyable from the start.

Even after the flavor began to fade, Orbit remained soft and pleasant to chew. It never developed that tough, waxy consistency that made some of the lower-ranked gums so unpleasant.

The mint flavor lasted four minutes and seven seconds, which was a significant improvement over Trident.

If we're judging these gums purely on how intense the flavor is when you first start chewing, 5 Gum wins. This had the biggest, boldest burst of spearmint flavor in the entire lineup. The initial mint sensation was noticeably more powerful than anything else I tried, making it an excellent choice for someone who likes their gum to pack a punch.

And thankfully, the flavor wasn't just strong for the first few seconds. It lasted an impressive seven minutes and six seconds before finally fading away, putting it among the longest-lasting gums in the test. The only thing keeping 5 Gum from the top spot was that two other brands held on just a little longer.

Ice Breakers delivered one of the most interesting experiences of the entire taste test because its intense cooling sensation and overall mint flavor seemed to have two different lifespans.

For the first two minutes and seven seconds, the gum delivered a powerful cooling effect that made my mouth feel especially refreshed. But even after that initial cooling sensation faded, the spearmint flavor kept going. In fact, I was able to chew it for another five minutes and two seconds before the flavor finally disappeared, bringing the total to seven minutes and nine seconds.

That's just three seconds longer than 5 Gum, making this an incredibly close competition.

I have to admit, Eclipse surprised me more than any other gum in this ranking. Going into the test, I wasn't expecting it to outlast every other brand, especially after experiencing the intense initial flavor of 5 Gum and the cooling sensation of Ice Breakers.

The spearmint flavor lasted an impressive seven minutes and 33 seconds before finally disappearing, making it the longest-lasting gum of the seven I tested. While 5 Gum delivered the strongest initial flavor and Ice Breakers impressed with its cooling effect, Eclipse ultimately won the competition that mattered most: longevity.

It outlasted Ice Breakers by 24 seconds and 5 Gum by 27 seconds. Those aren't enormous differences, but when you've spent this much time counting every second of mint flavor, they certainly count. Eclipse might not have been my most anticipated winner, but the numbers don't lie.

For just a hundred bucks, you get a satisfyingly soft pure cashmere sweater in a classic, relaxed fit, available in an impressively wide range of colors.
